Article Title: Scientists turn one of the world's hardest-to-recycle plastics into high-performance engine lubricant, giving stubborn PVC waste a valuable second life
Article Text:
Representative image

How scientists turn hard-to-recycle PVC waste into high-performance engine lubricant

Why PVC is notoriously difficult to recycle

A failed experiment helped researchers discover the lubricant route

Researchers tested the material and studied its production potential

PVC waste could become a feedstock for more sustainable lubricant production

One of the world's most difficult plastics to recycle could soon have a far more valuable second life. Scientists at Virginia Tech have developed a chemical method that converts polyvinyl chloride, or PVC, into polyalphaolefin, an important material used in high-performance lubricants including engine oil. The approach tackles a longstanding problem with PVC, which is difficult to recycle because of its chlorine content and the variety of additives found in different products. Instead of trying to preserve the original plastic, the researchers break its polymer chains down and transform the resulting molecules into a lubricant material. The work, published in Nature on August 5, could offer a new route for turning problematic plastic waste into a higher-value industrial product while potentially making lubricant production more sustainable.The Virginia Tech team, led by chemist and chemical engineer Guoliang "Greg" Liu, developed a process that chemically transforms PVC into polyalphaolefin, or PAO, a class of synthetic hydrocarbon material used as a base component in high-performance lubricants. The process starts by placing PVC in a solvent and adding aluminium trichloride and alpha olefins. The mixture is then heated to about 70°C, or 158°F, for three hours.After the reaction, the researchers extract an oil-like material from the solvent. The significance of the approach lies in its ability to move PVC beyond conventional recycling. Rather than producing another PVC product, the researchers use the plastic as a chemical feedstock for manufacturing a substantially different and potentially more valuable material. The resulting lubricant material was subsequently evaluated through collaborations with researchers outside Virginia Tech.PVC is widely used in products ranging from plumbing pipes and window components to credit cards and toys, but recycling it presents particular challenges. Unlike many common plastics, PVC contains chlorine within its polymer structure, while commercial PVC products can also contain different combinations of plasticisers, stabilisers, pigments, fillers and other additives. This variation makes it difficult to process discarded PVC as a uniform recycling stream. Large quantities therefore have limited recycling options and can end up being discarded. Liu's team approached the problem through chemical upcycling, which involves breaking polymer molecules apart and using them to create new chemicals or materials rather than simply remoulding the original plastic. The researchers' objective was to find a productive destination for PVC waste while extracting greater value from a material that is otherwise challenging to recycle.The lubricant breakthrough emerged after the team's initial strategy produced disappointing results. Researchers first explored whether the chlorine atoms in PVC could be replaced with other chemical groups to transform the polymer into different materials. The products remained soft and somewhat gooey, however, and did not have the properties the researchers were seeking. That led Liu to consider whether the polymer chains should instead be broken down much further. By continuing to break the PVC chains into smaller molecular segments, the team began producing materials with properties that pointed towards a different application. What initially looked like an unsuccessful attempt to modify PVC therefore became the clue that led the researchers towards lubricant production. Doctoral student Eric Munyaneza Nuwayo led the project, with graduate students Connor S. Thompson and Abby Civiello also contributing to the work.The team worked with researchers possessing expertise in several areas to determine whether the material they produced could perform as a lubricant and whether the process might eventually be practical at larger scales. Samples were sent to Ali Erdemir at Texas A&M University for testing, while William Goddard at Caltech contributed computational studies of the chemistry. Virginia Tech researcher Xi Chen carried out economic and production analysis to investigate how the process could potentially be expanded beyond laboratory experiments. These collaborations are important because producing an oil-like material from plastic is only the first step. A useful commercial lubricant must have appropriate performance characteristics, while an industrial recycling process must also be able to handle feedstock, chemical inputs, separation, energy use and production costs. The researchers' work therefore examines both the chemistry and the possibility of developing the process into a larger-scale manufacturing route.The researchers say their approach could address two problems at once by creating a new use for difficult-to-recycle PVC while providing an alternative route to lubricant production. The potential environmental benefit comes from treating discarded plastic as a source of valuable chemical feedstock instead of simply disposing of it. However, the development should not be interpreted as meaning that all PVC waste can immediately be converted into commercial engine oil. The process still needs to be assessed for wider feedstocks, scale-up, economic feasibility and its overall environmental footprint. The fate of chlorine and other components present in real-world PVC waste is also an important consideration when evaluating the technology. If these challenges can be addressed, the research could demonstrate how chemical upcycling can turn a problematic plastic waste stream into a useful industrial material, giving PVC a second life in an unexpected place: high-performance lubrication.
Article Summary: Scientists at Virginia Tech have developed a chemical method that converts polyvinyl chloride, or PVC, into polyalphaolefin, an important material used in high-performance lubricants including engine oil. The approach tackles a longstanding problem with PVC, which is difficult to recycle because of its chlorine content.

Article Title: US House passes bill to stop federal funding of universities boycotting Israel
Article Text:
The bill's sponsors said it was not intended to hinder academic speech or debate, but to prevent the targeting of Israel and ⁠Judaism (Photo: Reuters).

The US House of Representatives passed a bill on Thursday that blocks federal aid for universities boycotting Israel, but it needs to pass the Senate to become a law.The lower house, dominated by the republican majority, voted 237-169 in favour of the "Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act", amid growing criticism of Israel over actions in Gaza.According to news agency Reuters, Thursday's House vote was mostly along party lines, with just two republicans voting nay and 33 Democrats voting in favour.Democrat Representative from New York, Jerrold Nadler, said before the vote that while he opposed the global ‘boycott, divestment and sanctions (BDS) movement, he would ⁠vote no, as he supports the right to free expression."It is the only way to ensure speech I do agree with is equally protected," Nadler said.Notably, the global BDS movement is an attempt to isolate ⁠Israel over its alleged treatment of Palestinians.On October 7, 2023, an attack led by Hamas resulted in the deaths of approximately 1,200 people in Israel. According to the Gaza health ministry, Israeli attacks since then have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians.Israel’s hardliner stance is increasingly becoming a subject of global criticism, sparking protests on several university campuses in the US.The bill's sponsors said it was not intended to hinder academic speech or debate, but to prevent the targeting of Israel and ⁠Judaism, alleging that the protests were antisemitic and supported extremism.The protesters denied the allegation, saying advocacy for Palestinian rights and objections to the devastation in Gaza should not be equated with ‌antisemitism or ⁠support for extremism.
Article Summary: The US House of Representatives passed a bill on Thursday that blocks federal aid for universities boycotting Israel. The lower house, dominated by the republican majority, voted 237-169 in favour of the "Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act" The bill needs to pass the Senate to become a law.

Article Title: In 2023, Princeton researchers tested radiative cooling with natural ventilation and thermal mass, keeping a building 3.9°C below outdoor air
Article Text:
Image AI generated

How did the cooling roof work with natural ventilation

Image AI generated

How much cooler did the test box stay than outdoor air

What did the study reveal about passive radiative cooling

In 2023, researchers tested whether a building could be cooler than the air outside while still relying on natural ventilation. The experiment used two insulated boxes in California to study how radiative cooling, thermal mass and temperature-driven airflow could work together without fans or mechanical systems. The test box had an uninsulated aluminium roof covered with a radiative cooling material. According to the study published in Cell, titled ‘ Passive radiative cooling to sub-ambient temperatures inside naturally ventilated buildings ’, the surface released heat towards the sky, while its underside absorbed heat from inside the box through natural convection. Differences between indoor and outdoor temperatures drove air through the ventilation openings, and thermal mass helped moderate the temperature. During the November experiment, the test box was 3.9°C below the prevailing outdoor temperature, while the reference box was 5.0°C above it. Despite an internal heat source, the test box also maintained nearly seven air changes per hour during the day.The test box relied on temperature differences to move air instead of using fans. During the day, when the interior was cooler than the outside air, buoyancy forces produced a downward mixing flow through the box.The reference box used the opposite arrangement. Air moved upwards when the interior became warmer than the outdoor air.The roof was responsible for much of the heat rejection. Its radiative cooling surface released thermal energy towards the sky, while the underside transferred heat from the interior through natural convection. Thermal mass inside the box absorbed and released heat as temperatures changed. The researchers scaled the experiment to represent about one per cent of the ventilation rate and heat load associated with a single occupant, allowing the results to be considered in terms of building-scale conditions.The experiments were carried out under clear skies, with the researchers recording indoor temperatures, ventilation rates and heat flows. In November, the reference box was 5.0°C above the prevailing mean ambient temperature. The test box, in contrast, was 3.9°C below the prevailing mean. It also reduced the outdoor temperature swing by a factor of 0.59.The lower temperature was maintained while the test box continued exchanging air with the outside. During the day, it recorded nearly seven air changes per hour even with an internal heat source. Overall, the test box was 8.9°C cooler than the reference “gold standard” for passive cooling. Its temperature was less stable than that of the reference box because the roof radiator temperature varied with outdoor conditions.The experiment showed that radiative cooling could work alongside buoyancy-driven ventilation and thermal mass to keep indoor temperatures below the prevailing outdoor temperature. The test box was designed to distinguish the effect of radiative heat rejection from the effects of nighttime ventilation. Since it ventilated during the day rather than relying on night-time cooling, the researchers could examine the contribution of radiative cooling more directly.The researchers concluded that a naturally ventilated building could be cooled below the prevailing ambient temperature using an uninsulated roof that radiates heat towards the sky. Their calibrated model also suggested that adding thermal mass to the roof radiator could reduce temperature fluctuations while keeping the indoor temperature below the prevailing mean. The study combined radiative cooling, thermal mass and temperature-driven ventilation in a passive system that maintained air exchange without mechanical ventilation.
Article Summary: Researchers tested whether a building could be cooler than the air outside while still relying on natural ventilation. Experiment used two insulated boxes in California to study how radiative cooling, thermal mass and temperature-driven airflow could work together without fans or mechanical systems. The test box had an uninsulated aluminium roof covered with a radiative cooled material. Its surface released heat towards the sky, while its underside absorbed heat from inside the box through natural convection.

Article Title: Pine martens vanished from England for a century; locals built den boxes and set up cameras to track their return, now four kits have been spotted
Article Text:
Pine martens return to England after a century

19 pine martens were released on Exmoor

Local people helped track their return

A camera captured a female with four kits

Four kits offer hope for a self-sustaining population

Dartmoor’s pine martens are breeding too

Why conservationists want the predator back

The reintroduced animals are being closely monitored

The comeback remains vulnerable

Seven years of preparation are beginning to pay off

People are now being asked to help find more

Four kits mark the beginning, not the end

Pine martens are making a remarkable return to south-west England after disappearing from Exmoor for more than a century, with conservationists capturing the first confirmed evidence that the reintroduced animals are breeding in the wild. A remote trail camera recorded a female pine marten with four kits on Exmoor, signalling that an ambitious effort to restore the native predator is beginning to take hold. The breakthrough follows the release of 19 pine martens on Exmoor in September 2025 after years of preparation involving conservation organisations, landowners, volunteers and local communities. Volunteers have supported the project through practical conservation work, including helping with den boxes and monitoring wildlife cameras, while conservationists have tracked the released animals to understand how they are settling into the landscape. The sighting of four kits marks a major step towards establishing a self-sustaining population.Pine martens (Martes martes) were once widespread across Britain, including south-west England, but their numbers fell dramatically because of persecution, trapping, hunting and habitat loss. The species disappeared from Exmoor more than a century ago and became extremely rare across much of England. Their main remaining stronghold in Britain was Scotland, where healthier wild populations could support carefully selected animals for conservation translocations.The return to Exmoor is part of the Two Moors Pine Marten Project, which aims to restore the species across Dartmoor and Exmoor and eventually establish a connected population throughout south-west England. The project is led by Devon Wildlife Trust and involves Dartmoor National Park Authority, Exmoor National Park Authority, Forestry England, the National Trust, Somerset Wildlife Trust and the Woodland Trust, with expert support from the Vincent Wildlife Trust.The latest phase of the recovery began in September 2025, when 19 pine martens were released into woodland on Exmoor. The founding group consisted of nine females and 10 males, providing conservationists with a balanced starting population for the reintroduction. The animals came from healthy wild populations in the Scottish Highlands and underwent health checks before being transported to Devon. The release was the result of around seven years of preparation, including habitat assessments, discussions with landowners and farmers and planning for the animals' long-term monitoring. The pine martens were placed in specially prepared release pens before being allowed to explore the surrounding woodland. Each animal was fitted with a radio collar so project staff could track its movements and study how it used the new landscape.The reintroduction was led by conservation organisations, but local people have played an important role in supporting the recovery. Volunteers have helped with practical work such as constructing den boxes and assisting with wildlife monitoring. The project has also encouraged people across Devon, Cornwall and Somerset to report possible pine marten sightings, particularly when photographs are available. Trail cameras have become an especially important monitoring tool because pine martens are elusive and mainly active at night or around dusk and dawn. Remote cameras allow conservationists to record animals without disturbing them and can reveal behaviour that would be difficult to observe directly. The involvement of local people therefore gives the project a much wider network for detecting animals as they move beyond the areas where conservationists are actively tracking them.The major breakthrough came when one of the project's remote trail cameras recorded a female pine marten with four young kits. The cameras are positioned across the landscape to monitor the reintroduced animals, with some using scents and food such as peanut butter and fish oil to attract pine martens close enough to be recorded. The footage provides the first confirmed evidence that the reintroduced population on Exmoor has successfully bred. That makes the discovery considerably more significant than an ordinary wildlife sighting. An adult surviving after release would demonstrate that the animal had adapted to its surroundings, but a female raising young shows that at least one of the reintroduced animals has survived, reproduced and found conditions suitable for raising the next generation.The discovery of four kits is particularly encouraging because pine martens generally have relatively small litters. Females usually give birth in March or April, and two or three kits are typical, although larger litters can occur. Ali North, the Two Moors Pine Marten Project's field officer for Exmoor, said the team had been monitoring the animals and was delighted to see evidence of breeding. Ali Hawkins, senior ecologist at Exmoor National Park Authority, described the breeding evidence as a major milestone while stressing that the population remains small and vulnerable. The kits therefore do not mean that the reintroduction is complete. Instead, they provide the first clear indication that the population has moved beyond simple survival after release and has begun the crucial process of reproduction.The Exmoor discovery follows an earlier success on neighbouring Dartmoor. The Two Moors Pine Marten Project released 15 pine martens on Dartmoor in autumn 2024, consisting of eight females and seven males. Trail-camera footage subsequently confirmed that females had produced young. In 2026, further footage showed a female with two kits near the Wray Valley, providing evidence of breeding for a second consecutive year. The breeding records from both Dartmoor and Exmoor are encouraging because the project's wider objective is to establish viable populations in both landscapes. If those populations expand and animals disperse between suitable areas, they could eventually help create a much larger and more connected population across the south-west.Pine martens are native woodland predators and omnivores that eat a broad range of foods, including small mammals, birds, insects and fruit. Their return restores a predator that had been missing from parts of south-west England for generations. Conservationists are also interested in their potential influence on grey squirrels. Research elsewhere in Britain has found relationships between recovering pine marten populations and grey squirrel abundance, and pine martens may create conditions that benefit native red squirrels in some landscapes. However, it would be premature to claim that the Exmoor reintroduction will automatically control grey squirrels or restore red squirrels. The central aim of the project is to restore a native species and rebuild ecological processes that were disrupted when pine martens disappeared.Conservationists are using several methods to determine whether the animals are adapting and establishing themselves. Radio collars fitted to the released pine martens allow researchers to follow individual movements and determine which habitats they use. Remote cameras provide information on activity, behaviour and breeding, while public reports can reveal animals outside the project's main monitoring areas. This combination is particularly useful for a species that is difficult to observe directly. Monitoring will also help conservationists identify potential threats and understand whether the population is expanding naturally. The evidence gathered during the early years of the project will be important in determining whether the animals can survive and reproduce without further releases.Despite the excitement surrounding the four kits, conservationists say the population is still small and vulnerable. Pine martens naturally occur at relatively low densities and produce only one litter each year, so population growth can be gradual. The animals also face modern threats, including road deaths and accidental poisoning from rodenticides. Habitat connectivity will become increasingly important if young pine martens disperse into new areas. Conservationists therefore need to continue monitoring the population and working with landowners and local communities to make sure suitable habitat remains available. The four kits are a sign that the project is moving in the right direction, but they are not proof that the species has yet secured a permanent foothold.The return of pine martens to Exmoor was not a quick reintroduction exercise. The Two Moors Pine Marten Project spent roughly seven years preparing for the releases, assessing habitats, working with landowners and farmers and developing systems for monitoring the animals. Volunteers and local communities became part of that wider effort by supporting practical conservation work and helping gather information about wildlife. The release of 19 animals in 2025 was therefore one stage in a much longer conservation programme. The discovery of the four kits now provides evidence that the years of planning and monitoring are producing the outcome conservationists ultimately wanted, with reintroduced animals surviving in the wild and producing a new generation.The conservation effort is continuing, and members of the public are being encouraged to report possible pine marten sightings across Devon, Cornwall and Somerset. Photographs can help experts distinguish pine martens from other similarly sized mammals and verify records. People who already operate trail cameras are also being encouraged to take part in wildlife monitoring. This public involvement could become increasingly valuable as young pine martens grow and begin dispersing from their mother's territory. Each verified sighting can help conservationists understand how far the population is spreading and whether animals are beginning to establish themselves beyond the original release sites.A female pine marten moving through Exmoor woodland with four kits is a striking sign of a species returning after generations of absence. The footage provides the first confirmed evidence that the animals released on Exmoor have bred and that the landscape is supporting their young. For the conservationists and volunteers involved, it is an important reward for years of preparation, monitoring and practical work. But the real measure of success will come over the years ahead, as more young are born, animals disperse and the population becomes capable of sustaining itself. After more than a century without pine martens, however, the appearance of four kits offers a powerful early sign that England's lost woodland predator is beginning to reclaim part of its former range.
Article Summary: Pine martens were once widespread across Britain, including south-west England. Their numbers fell dramatically because of persecution, trapping, hunting and habitat loss. The species disappeared from Exmoor more than a century ago and became extremely rare across much of England. The sighting of four kits marks a major step towards establishing a self-sustaining population.

Article Title: Scientists removed just 20–40% of fish from a degraded Chinese lake; underwater plants and water clarity began recovering
Article Text:
Representative Image of a pristine highland lake transitioning from murky water to clear, with submerged plants thriving (AI Generated Image)

Why researchers removed particular fish from Caohai Lake

What happened to the lake after the fish were removed

How reducing fish pressure helped underwater plants return

Why the experiment could change how degraded lakes are restored

Caohai Lake, a highland lake in southwest China, began losing its underwater vegetation after 2016. By 2019, submerged plants covered less than 10 per cent of the lake, down from around 70 per cent just a few years earlier. The change was part of a wider deterioration in the lake, with murkier water and more phytoplankton taking the place of the clear, plant-filled conditions. Researchers wanted to see whether the lake could be pushed back towards its earlier state without removing most of its fish. Between February 2022 and July 2023, they removed about 55 kilograms of fish per hectare, equal to roughly 20 to 40 per cent of the lake's fish biomass. The fish were not taken out at random. Researchers focused on benthic omnivores, herbivores and zooplanktivores that could eat plants, disturb the sediment or affect the animals that feed on algae. After the removal, underwater plants increased, and several other parts of the lake's ecosystem changed with them.The study, published in the Journal of Environmental Management titled Moderately intensive selective fish removal enhances biodiversity and promotes ecosystem restoration: a whole-lake experiment , stated that the fish removal was aimed at species that were putting pressure on the lake's vegetation and food web.Researchers targeted groups including benthic omnivores, herbivores and zooplanktivores, rather than simply taking out as many fish as possible. Two species that had become dominant, Carassius auratus, the crucian carp, and Hemiculter leucisculus, declined significantly after the intervention. Other fish and benthic macroinvertebrates also became more diverse. The researchers linked the changes to the idea behind the Intermediate Disturbance Hypothesis, which holds that moderate disturbance can sometimes prevent a few species from dominating an ecosystem and leave room for more species to coexist. In Caohai, the aim was not to empty the lake of fish, but to reduce the species putting the most pressure on the existing plant community.The biggest visible change was in the submerged plants. Their coverage increased by 29 percent, while their biomass increased by 428 grams per square metre. At the same time, phytoplankton biomass fell by 6.7 milligrams per litre and chlorophyll-a concentrations dropped by 38.3 micrograms per litre. Water transparency also improved by 15 centimetres, allowing light to travel farther into the lake. Fish and benthic macroinvertebrate communities both recorded increases in alpha diversity. In other words, the changes were not limited to the plants growing back. The researchers saw shifts in several parts of the lake's food web at the same time, along with improvements in measures of water quality.The researchers used partial least squares path modelling to look at how the different changes in the lake were connected. Their analysis pointed towards reduced fish pressure on submerged macrophytes as one possible explanation for the recovery. Some of the fish removed during the experiment could graze on plants, disturb bottom sediments or alter the food web through their feeding habits. With fewer of these fish present, the plants faced less pressure and were able to expand. More vegetation can in turn help keep sediments in place and improve conditions for clearer water, while also changing the habitat available to other aquatic organisms. The modelling supports this chain of events, but the researchers did not claim that fish removal alone explains every change in the lake. Caohai had already been affected by several pressures, so the recovery cannot be reduced to a single factor.What makes the Caohai experiment interesting is how much changed after a relatively limited fish removal. Researchers removed roughly 20 to 40 percent of the lake's standing fish biomass rather than carrying out a near-total fish cull. The intervention was followed by the return of more submerged vegetation, greater diversity among fish and bottom-dwelling invertebrates, lower phytoplankton levels and clearer water. That does not mean Caohai has been permanently restored. The study covered the intervention from 2022 to 2023, and the researchers say longer monitoring is needed to find out whether the changes will last. Fish populations can recover after removal, and the pressures that originally pushed the lake into a degraded state can return. For now, however, the experiment shows that a targeted reduction in fish can be followed by changes across an entire lake ecosystem, giving restoration managers another approach to consider for degraded plateau lakes.

By 2019, submerged plants covered less than 10 per cent of the lake, down from around 70 per cent just a few years earlier. Researchers wanted to see whether the lake could be pushed back towards its earlier state without removing most of its fish. Researchers focused on benthic omnivores, herbivores and zooplanktivores that could eat plants, disturb the sediment or affect the animals

Article Title: At 9, Yonas Hagos arrived in America from a Sudan refugee camp; years later, he became a major Arby’s franchise owner after serving in the US Army
Article Text:
Image: Inspire Stories

Yonas Hagos arrived in America as a refugee child

From fast-food worker to US Army Purple Heart recipient

After the Army, Yonas Hagos pursued his dream of owning a business

Yonas Hagos became an Arby’s franchise owner after growing up poor

At nine years old, Yonas Hagos arrived in America after spending part of his childhood in a refugee camp in Sudan. He spoke little English and entered a life that was dramatically different from the one his family had known. In Illinois, Hagos and his four siblings shared a small two-bedroom apartment with their parents, who worked whatever jobs they could find to support the family. As a teenager, he began working in fast food and taking on odd jobs to earn money. Years later, the attacks of September 11 changed the direction of his life. Hagos enlisted in the US Army in 2002 and eventually served in Iraq, where he was critically wounded by a rocket-propelled grenade. He survived, recovered and received the Purple Heart. After leaving the military, he pursued another childhood ambition, becoming a business owner, eventually building a multi-brand franchise operation that included Arby’s.Yonas Hagos' journey began long before he became a franchise owner. In 1992, he travelled with his parents and four siblings from a refugee camp in Sudan to Chicago, beginning a new life in America.Hagos was only nine years old and remembered being amazed by everything around him, from the size of American houses to the speed of the cars. His family settled in Wheaton, Illinois, in a two-bedroom Section 8 apartment, with the children sharing two twin beds. According to Inspire Brands, Hagos grew up poor but watched his parents work relentlessly to provide for their family. That example shaped his own attitude towards work. At 14, he obtained permission to take his first fast-food job and also earned money by shovelling driveways, cutting grass and taking whatever work was available.Hagos continued working in restaurants while attending high school and college, but his path changed after the September 11 attacks. Wanting to give something back to the country that had given his family a new opportunity, he decided to join the US Army. He enlisted in 2002, serving overseas in Germany and Kuwait before being deployed to Iraq in 2004. During his final tour, Hagos was travelling through Baghdad in a Howitzer when his unit came under attack. An RPG struck the vehicle, leaving him severely wounded and without a detectable pulse. His comrades initially considered him killed in action before he regained consciousness nearly a minute later. He underwent numerous surgeries and began rehabilitation in Germany. Doctors initially told him he might have only 50% mobility, but after a difficult recovery he ultimately reached about 95%. Hagos received the Purple Heart Medal for his injuries.Surviving his injuries gave Hagos a renewed determination to pursue the ambition he had carried since childhood, becoming a businessman. He first established a painting company to save enough money to enter the franchise industry. His first franchised business was a 24-hour health and fitness club, which he purchased in 2009. From there, his operation grew rapidly. At one point, Hagos owned 17 Dunkin’ restaurants, demonstrating that the discipline and persistence he developed during his military career could translate into entrepreneurship. He eventually expanded into other restaurant brands, including Smoothie King, Chicken Salad Chick and Arby’s. His experience was built gradually rather than overnight, with each business providing the foundation for the next. His approach was rooted in hard work, patience and a willingness to follow established systems while continuing to look for opportunities to grow.Arby’s had a personal connection for Hagos because he had grown up eating at the chain in Wheaton. After hearing a business associate discuss the brand, he returned to an Arby’s restaurant, tried its brisket and began considering the company as another opportunity for expansion. He travelled to Atlanta to meet Arby’s leadership and said the brand's vision convinced him to become part of its growth. Hagos opened his first Arby’s restaurant in 2019. His story had by then travelled a remarkable distance, from a refugee camp in Sudan and a crowded apartment in Illinois to military service, a Purple Heart and ownership of multiple restaurant businesses. His journey is an example of perseverance and the possibilities created through franchising. His career demonstrates how a childhood shaped by poverty and displacement ultimately became the foundation for a life built around work, service and entrepreneurship.
Article Summary: Yonas Hagos grew up poor in a refugee camp in Sudan. At 14, he took his first fast-food job and earned money by shovelling driveways, cutting grass and taking whatever work was available. He enlisted in the US Army in 2002 and eventually served in Iraq, where he was critically wounded by a rocket-propelled grenade. Hagos received the Purple Heart Medal for his injuries. After leaving the military, he pursued his dream of owning a business. He eventually built a multi-brand franchise operation that included Arby’s.

Article Title: Texas mom says school told her staff caught her 5-year-old son; she later learned a stranger found him crying two blocks away
Article Text:
Representative image

A good Samaritan helps

Representative image

The school has a different story

Mother demands action

Representative image

Kindergarten student leaves school without anyone noticing; a good Samaritan brings the child back after her ‘mom instincts’ kick in, but the school has a different storyA five-year-old kindergarten student in Texas left the school in the middle of the day without anyone noticing, before being found by a good Samaritan who safely returned the child to campus, WFAA reported.The student, Elijah, left Rufino Mendoza Elementary School in Fort Worth, Texas, during school hours on Monday, August 31, NBC 5 reported. The child was later discovered by Isabel Barrera several blocks away, crying in the street. She was in the neighbourhood visiting her parents when she found him. She noticed the school name on the boy’s shirt and drove him back to campus, where staff told her they had no idea he was gone.“I see a little boy in the street; he’s running, crying, and I think my mom instincts just kicked in. He hugged me, and I hugged him back, and I was like, ‘Are you OK?’ And at that point, all I could think about was, he’s someone’s baby,” Barrera told the outlet.According to her, the school didn’t even know that the student had gone missing. “They’re like, OK, and everybody starts freaking out; they’re like, ‘Oh my God, we didn’t even know he got out,’” she added.Fort Worth ISD didn’t clarify how a student could leave the campus or how long the kindergartener was away from the school.“Fort Worth ISD is aware of an incident involving a kindergarten student who left campus during lunch on Monday. The student was safely located by a community member and promptly returned to school,” they said in a statement to WFAA. “The safety and well-being of our students remain our highest priority.”The district and campus administration are currently looking into the circumstances that led to the incident. Necessary steps to strengthen the existing safety protocols and procedures will be taken, according to the district.The child’s mother, Rebekah Alcaraz, said school officials gave her a completely different account when she arrived at pickup. “They said that he had walked out of the building but that two employees and the security guard had got to him before he was able to leave, and they brought him back inside,” she told NBC5.The mother later saw a post by Barrera’s husband in a neighbourhood Facebook group and realised that a stranger had found her son on the streets.Alcaraz and Elijah’s grandmother met with school and district staff on Tuesday, but they felt their concerns were not being taken seriously.“I feel like we’re being dismissed,” Alcaraz said.The mother added that the incident has left her worried about the safety of her son at the school. “They traumatized my little boy. They traumatized me as a parent, and I fear for his safety now at that school.”Though the school assured Barrera that the child’s family would be notified of the incident, the mother claims they didn’t tell her the whole story.“What they failed to tell me was that my son left the school campus. He was three to four blocks away from the school; he was crying and lost out there. And a parent that just so happened to have seen him was the one who brought him back. They didn’t notify me of any of this,” Alcaraz told the Fort Worth Star-Telegram.In the Facebook post, Barrera’s husband asked the school to do better on student safety protocols. “FWISD and Rufino Mendoza Elementary need to do better.”According to the outlet, the child’s mother has filed a police report and is also planning to seek legal action against the district. “It’s a parent’s worst nightmare, and it’s something you don’t think could ever happen to you until that happens to you. The fact that they’re not taking accountability still — that’s what’s really getting to me,” Alcaraz said.The incident has put a spotlight on whether the district’s heavily funded turnaround effort is reaching campus operations. For parents like Alcaraz, the money spent on teacher salaries and instructional overhauls means little if their child can walk out unnoticed.
Article Summary: Elijah, 5, left Rufino Mendoza Elementary School in Fort Worth, Texas, during school hours on Monday, August 31. The child was later discovered by Isabel Barrera several blocks away, crying in the street. She noticed the school name on the boy’s shirt and drove him back to campus, where staff told her they had no idea he was gone.

Article Title: Magnitude 5 quake hits Tibet amid ongoing search for hundreds missing after deadly floods
Article Text:
Earthquake strikes Tibet (representative image)

Nepal flood toll rises to 1,252; over 4,200 still missing

Poll Vote & Share your view Which area do you believe needs the most immediate focus in rescue operations? Hydropower tunnels Areas affected by landslides Flood-impacted towns Rescue of foreign citizens 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

An earthquake of magnitude 5 struck Tibet on Thursday, according to the German Research Centre for Geosciences (GFZ).The quake occurred at a depth of 10 km (6.21 miles), GFZ said.The earthquake struck as rescue and recovery operations continued in Tibet following catastrophic flooding near the Gyirong border crossing with Nepal last week.China on Wednesday fully reopened the only road leading to the Gyirong crossing after sections of it were washed away, allowing heavy machinery to reach the main disaster zone for the first time, Reuters reported.The damage to the G216 national highway had earlier forced authorities to airdrop equipment and supplies to frontline rescuers, while some teams trekked through the mountains to reach the affected area.China's official death toll from the flooding in Tibet had risen to 21 by Wednesday, with 541 people still missing, according to Reuters.The missing included 104 Nepali citizens, 49 Indians, 33 Latvians and six Canadians, authorities had previously said.Rescue operations have been hampered by persistent rain, unstable cliffs and the fast-flowing river in the narrow mountain gorge, though authorities said the risks from monitored upstream lakes had diminished.Landslides, however, remained a concern.Across the border, Nepal's flash flood death toll has risen to 1,252, while around 4,216 people remain missing or out of contact, according to the latest update issued by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) on Thursday.The highest number of bodies has been recovered from Chitwan, at 355, followed by Nawalparasi East with 218, Nawalparasi West with 208, Nuwakot with 177 and Rasuwa with 127. Bodies have also been recovered from Gorkha, Dhading and Tanahun.Only 95 bodies have so far been identified and handed over to relatives, according to the NDRRMA.Around 11,993 people have been rescued and 5,135 injured people have received medical treatment. The missing include about 900 people linked to hydroelectric projects, as well as around 583 foreign citizens and 164 Nepalis accompanying foreign tourists.Search and rescue operations remain focused on areas affected by landslides, floodwaters and debris, with more than 21,000 security personnel deployed for rescue, search and relief operations.Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on hydropower tunnels, where authorities believe some of the missing workers may have survived after being cut off by floodwaters and debris, Reuters reported.“We are very confident that there is life in there because ... there is food and water in the building, that was likely built for communication purposes and as a resting place,” Amshu Kiran Shahi, a board member of the Nepal Electricity Authority, told Reuters.Nepal foreign minister Shisir Khanal, meanwhile, described the disaster as a “Himalayan Tsunami” while briefing diplomats in Kathmandu on Thursday.“I want to call the disaster the Himalayan Tsunami as we have not experienced such a massive disaster in our recent memory,” Khanal said.The flash floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastated towns and villages across northern and central Nepal.Specialised rescue teams from India, China and the United States were involved in tunnel rescue attempts.Meanwhile, Nepal plans to rebuild an early-warning system for landslides along part of its border with China after the glacial flood swept away existing monitoring infrastructure, Reuters reported, citing two Nepali government sources.The new system is expected to include seismic sensors, cameras and a satellite link to help authorities monitor fresh hazards and issue warnings.The immediate danger from two barrier lakes near the border has passed after they drained, but the terrain remains unstable and is being closely watched.
Article Summary: An earthquake of magnitude 5 struck Tibet on Thursday, according to the German Research Centre for Geosciences. Rescue and recovery operations continued in Tibet following catastrophic flooding near the Gyirong border crossing with Nepal last week. China's official death toll from the flooding in Tibet had risen to 21 by Wednesday, with 541 people still missing.

Article Title: US struck 60 targets as 40 vessels, 18mn barrels of oil crossed Hormuz in record day: Report
Article Text:
The operation comes amid growing risks for commercial shipping

The US military escorted 40 commercial vessels carrying around 18 million barrels of oil through the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, marking a wartime high as Washington and Tehran exchanged a fresh round of strikes, according to two US officials familiar with the operation who spoke to CNN.The high-risk operation came as US forces simultaneously struck nearly 60 Iranian military targets around the strategic waterway, while defending the escorted vessels against waves of drone attacks and neutralising anti-ship cruise missiles.Before the war began just over six months ago, around 20 million barrels of oil passed through the Strait of Hormuz each day. But since the conflict began, shipping through the key waterway has slowed to a trickle, disrupting global energy markets and pushing up prices.The US operation involved a range of air, sea and space assets and was part of a broader strategy focused on controlling the strait, protecting commercial shipping and increasing economic pressure on Iran.The targets hit on Tuesday included air defence sites, radar systems, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities and communications sites, the officials told CNN. US forces also continued a naval blockade of Iranian ports, with Central Command directed to focus its efforts on the strait and preventing oil exports from leaving or entering Iranian ports.The operation comes amid growing risks for commercial shipping. On Monday, a Saudi Arabia-flagged crude oil tanker came under attack and caught fire as it was preparing to cross the strait, killing two Filipino crew members. Fourteen other Filipino crew members survived.Iran has also stepped up attacks on US allies in the Gulf. Bahrain said its air defence systems intercepted several Iranian air attacks early Wednesday, while Iranian state media reported drone attacks on US bases in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates.The escalation followed US strikes on Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday. Washington said Iran was preparing to use the launchers to fire mines into the waterway. Iran retaliated by launching missiles at American bases in Jordan, which were intercepted.The US military’s latest operation, however, has not eased concerns among energy companies about sending ships through the strait, even under military escort. Energy prices remain elevated, adding to turbulence in global markets.At the same time, the administration’s other priorities have taken a back seat. According to one US official, operations aimed at eliminating elements of Iran’s nuclear programme have effectively been “backburnered”, as the focus shifts towards securing the waterway and restricting Iranian oil flows.Iranian media meanwhile reported that a US strike hit a home hosting a wedding in Kuhestak, killing four people and wounding at least 68. The US military said it was aware of the report but that it “never targets civilians.”With the conflict intensifying, diplomatic efforts are continuing. Egypt and Qatar have called for Washington and Tehran to return to negotiations, while Pakistan said it remains engaged in mediation efforts. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also said Washington was pressuring countries still doing business with Iran, saying, “My message to everyone is stay away.”
Article Summary: The US military escorted 40 commercial vessels carrying around 18 million barrels of oil through the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. US forces simultaneously struck nearly 60 Iranian military targets around the strategic waterway, while defending the escorted vessels against waves of drone attacks and neutralising anti-ship cruise missiles.

Article Title: Too many allies? Why Netanyahu's far-right partners are hurting him in upcoming Israel polls
Article Text:
Netanyahu’s far-right allies in Israel are posing biggest challenge for him

Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing an unusual threat ahead of the October 27 election: divisions within the far-right bloc that support his government.Smotrich’s Religious Zionism and Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power, which ran together in the 2022 elections, have rejected Netanyahu's calls for another merger amid tensions. Meanwhile, smaller parties led by former Likud members and former general Ofer Winter are competing for the same right-wing voters, deepening fragmentation.“When we unite, we win. When we split up, we lose,” Netanyahu told Israel's local media outlet Channel 14, according to AP.Netanyahu currently heads a coalition of religious and ultranationalist parties.Netanyahu’s Likud party on Friday rebuked national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir for refusing to run on a joint slate with finance minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party, warning that a divided vote could weaken the coalition’s chances of retaining power.Several smaller parties are competing for the same right-wing electorate, raising the prospect that some could fall below Israel’s electoral threshold and leave their votes without parliamentary representation.Under Israel’s electoral system, parties must secure at least 3.25 per cent of the vote to win representation in the 120-member Knesset. A party that falls below the threshold receives no seats, making fragmentation particularly consequential for Netanyahu’s bloc.The Financial Times reported that Netanyahu has sparred publicly with Ben-Gvir, who rejected a meeting this week to discuss a merger with Smotrich. Ben-Gvir accused the prime minister of an “attempt to weaken” his Jewish Power party.Netanyahu responded by urging Ben-Gvir to “not burn tens of thousands of rightwing votes . . . and crown a leftwing government”, while also telling him to “overcome your personal ego”.Ben-Gvir, however, argues that a merger could cost his party seats. “According to all the polls, a connection between me and Smotrich distances Jewish Strength by 3-4 mandates who won't come to vote, and the right-wing government will fall!” he wrote on X.The dispute has left Netanyahu pressing harder for unity. In a video posted on X, he said Smotrich and Ben-Gvir “must unite. Every time we ran united, we won. When we ran separately, we lost.”“In 1992, the Right had more votes than the Left, like today, but because we were running separately, we got the disaster of Oslo, Arafat, Hamas and recurring catastrophes,” Netanyahu said, referring to the peace process launched through the Oslo Accords.Smotrich appeared more receptive, writing on X, “It's time for unity and responsibility in the national camp.”Netanyahu subsequently invited Ben-Gvir and Smotrich to meet on Sunday, saying, “We must not waste a single vote; we must unite to save the right-wing bloc!”The stakes are high for Netanyahu, whose nearly uninterrupted 17 years in power are being tested in an election shaped by the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack, mass protests and wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.The parties have until September 8 to decide whether to merge, withdraw or contest the election separately.
Article Summary: Netanyahu currently heads a coalition of religious and ultranationalist parties. The parties have until September 8 to decide whether to merge, withdraw or contest the election separately. Several smaller parties are competing for the same right-wing electorate, raising the prospect that some could fall below Israel's electoral threshold and leave their votes without parliamentary representation.

Article Title: Australia planted eucalyptus trees to fight rising soil salinity; decades later scientists found the plantations were changing groundwater but not the soil nature
Article Text:
Eucalyptus cladocalyx ‘nana’. Image Credit: ERA Nurseries

How did eucalyptus plantations change groundwater and soil salinity in Australia

The groundwater changed, but the saline seep remained

Why didn't the eucalyptus trees solve the salinity problem

Image Credit: AI generated

Some eucalyptus species performed better over 15 years

nana

A long-term lesson from Australia's eucalyptus plantations

Australia planted eucalyptus trees to fight rising soil salinity, hoping that thirsty, deep-rooted vegetation could help control the groundwater processes behind the problem. A long-running experiment in south-western Australia later showed that the effects of such plantations were more complicated than simply planting trees and waiting for the land to recover. Researchers established a mixed eucalyptus plantation above a saline seep in 1976 and monitored how the trees affected groundwater levels and salt movement for 15 years. The study found clear signs that the plantation used more water than nearby crops and pasture, while groundwater conditions also changed over time. Yet the trees did not stop the saline seep as researchers had hoped. Published in ‘ Agricultural Water Management ,’ this comprehensive study reveals that effective land management requires understanding complex underground hydrological systems, cautioning against oversimplified solutions to persistent environmental challenges like soil salinity.The study examined a plantation established on about 12% of a small farm catchment. The trees were planted above a saline seep, an area where salty groundwater had reached or approached the surface and damaged the land. The researchers wanted to identify eucalyptus species that could use large amounts of water and potentially help reclaim such affected areas. According to the study, the catchment contained two important groundwater systems.One was a deep aquifer in the lower part of the landscape and the other, a shallower seasonal aquifer. The researchers monitored changes in groundwater level and salinity using piezometers, allowing them to follow how conditions changed as the plantation developed.The results showed that the plantation was having a noticeable effect on water use. Changes in groundwater levels, along with observations of perched water, indicated that the trees were using more water than the nearby crop and pasture vegetation. This was an important finding because the basic idea behind planting trees in salt-affected agricultural landscapes was that trees could alter the movement of water through the soil. If less water moved downwards into the groundwater system, or if trees removed more water from the landscape, they could potentially help limit the processes that bring salt towards the surface.The researchers found that the plantation influenced groundwater chemistry as well as water levels. Chloride concentrations in the deep aquifer fell by approximately 20% between 1977 and 1984. The decline was greater at the middle of the slope than further downslope. This suggested that conditions beneath the catchment were changing, although the changes were not uniform across the landscape. At the same time, the study found larger stores of salt in the soil downslope than at the middle of the slope. There was also visual evidence that salt continued to be discharged extensively through the saline seep throughout the experiment. In other words, the trees were clearly affecting the local water system, but their presence did not bring the expected recovery of the seep. The research showed why this distinction matters. A plantation may increase water use and change groundwater conditions without having enough influence over the particular underground system responsible for a saline area. The findings also suggested that surface changes alone could not explain what was happening beneath the catchment, where groundwater pathways controlled the movement of salt.One of the most important findings of the study concerned the location of the plantation. The researchers identified the site's underground geology as a significant reason why the trees failed to control the seepage. The plantation was located in an area where the relevant aquifer appeared to be ‘confined.’ That meant the groundwater system beneath the site was not easy for the trees to influence in the way researchers had hoped. This finding highlighted a practical limitation of tree-based approaches to salinity. Planting species that use substantial amounts of water may not be enough on its own. The location of groundwater, the way water moves through underground layers and the position of the plantation within the wider landscape can all affect the outcome. The study therefore showed that managing salinity is not simply a question of selecting the thirstiest trees. Understanding the underground environment is equally important.The experiment also compared the performance of different eucalyptus species. The original aim was to rank species partly according to water use, which the researchers assessed through factors including leaf area and survival. Tree growth was rapid during the early years of the experiment, continuing strongly until 1981. After that, growth declined. 15 years later, four species emerged as the most promising among those tested. These included ‘Eucalyptus cladocalyx var.,’ ‘Eucalyptus cladocalyx,’ ‘Eucalyptus occidentalis’ and ‘Eucalyptus sargentii.’ Their performance did not mean that the plantation had solved the saline seep problem. Instead, it showed that some species were better suited than others to the demanding conditions of the site. A tree can survive well and use considerable amounts of water while still being unable to alter a groundwater system enough to stop salt from reaching the surface.The 15-year experiment provided a more realistic picture of what tree planting could not achieve in salt-affected farmland. The eucalyptus plantation used more water than the surrounding vegetation, and conditions in the deep groundwater system also shifted, including a significant fall in chloride concentration. Yet the saline seep continued to discharge salt. As per the study, this outcome was due to the underground conditions beneath the plantation. The research pointed towards a broader lesson that the success of planting trees depends not only on the trees, but also on the landscape in which they are planted. For areas struggling with rising groundwater and soil salinity, the findings suggest that planting eucalyptus can be a useful tool, but it is not a solution. Trees can change groundwater behaviour, without necessarily controlling the source of the problem. Only by monitoring the plantation for many years were researchers able to see both the benefits of greater tree water use and the limits imposed by the site's hidden groundwater system.
Article Summary: Australia planted eucalyptus trees to fight rising soil salinity. Researchers monitored how the trees affected groundwater levels and salt movement for 15 years. The study found clear signs that the plantation used more water than nearby crops and pasture, while groundwater conditions also changed over time. Yet the trees did not stop the saline seep as researchers had hoped.

Article Title: In 2020, the US removed 69 dams, reconnecting 624 miles of rivers and restoring habitat for salmon, steelhead and native fish species
Article Text:
PC: American Rivers

US dam removals in 2020 addressed safety, ageing infrastructure and river restoration

Why removal of obsolete dams became US priority

How a 2020 dam removal restored 16 miles of salmon habitat

Dam removals across the US reopened rivers and restored vital fish habitat

The wider impact of 69 US dam removals in 2020

Across the United States, some rivers are beginning to flow through places where dams once stood. In 2020, 69 dams were removed across 23 states, reopening hundreds of miles of waterways that had been blocked for decades. Some structures had outlived the purpose for which they were built, while others had become expensive to maintain or posed growing safety concerns. For fish and wildlife, the changes could be significant, restoring access to stretches of river that had long been cut off. The work continued even as the Covid-19 pandemic disrupted construction and restoration projects across the country.According to American Rivers, from an obsolete industrial dam in Indiana to barriers affecting salmon habitat in Washington, the removals showed how decisions about ageing infrastructure can also reshape rivers, habitats and nearby communities. By the end of the year, the total number of dam removals in the US since 1912 had reached 1,797.The 69 removals recorded in 2020 brought the number of dams taken out across the US since 1912 to 1,797. Ohio recorded the highest number that year, with 11 removals, while Massachusetts and New York each recorded six, as reported.The work did not stop when normal construction schedules were disrupted by Covid-19. Engineers, contractors, local authorities, conservation groups and other partners continued with projects where it was possible to do so safely.There was no single reason for taking a dam out. In some places, a structure had become obsolete. Elsewhere, the issue was public safety, fish passage or the cost of maintaining ageing infrastructure. A few projects combined several of these concerns.More than 90,000 dams are estimated to stand across rivers in the US. They range from major pieces of infrastructure to relatively small barriers that were built for mills, water supplies, recreation or other local purposes.As these structures age, their original uses can disappear while the costs and risks associated with keeping them remain. Some also interfere with the movement of fish and alter the flow and ecological character of rivers.According to American Rivers, the failure of Michigan's Edenville Dam in May 2020 brought the safety issue into sharp focus. The collapse led to extensive flooding and became another reminder of the risks associated with ageing infrastructure. Reportedly, a United Nations report published around the same period also warned about the growing problems posed by ageing dams and water infrastructure.In many cases, the work is also tied to local economic activity. A study from the University of North Carolina estimated that ecological restoration directly employed about 126,000 people nationally and supported another 100,000 jobs indirectly, with the sector contributing around $25 billion to the US economy each year.One of the larger examples from 2020 took place on the Middle Fork Nooksack River near Bellingham, Washington.There, an old water diversion dam was removed and a new water intake installed. The change opened roughly 16 miles of previously inaccessible habitat for salmon. It also addressed cultural resources and maintained a dependable source of clean water for Bellingham.The project brought together a number of organisations, including American Rivers, the Nooksack Indian Tribe, the Lummi Nation and the City of Bellingham, alongside private funding from the Paul G. Allen Family Foundation and other partners.In New Hampshire’s White Mountain National Forest, a 21-foot concrete and earth dam once blocked the South Branch Gale River after being built in 1955 by the Littleton Water and Light Department as part of a water-supply system. By 2020, the dam was no longer in use, and its removal restored connectivity to about 15 miles of river upstream and 21 miles downstream.In South Carolina, the Burson Lake Dam on Reedy Creek faced a different problem after heavy rainfall damaged its spillway in spring 2020, increasing the risk of failure; rather than repair the ageing recreation dam, the US Forest Service chose to remove it, eliminating a safety concern and future maintenance costs while restoring habitat for aquatic species such as Bartram’s bass. In Indiana, the Elkhart River Dam, built around 1890 to divert water into raceways that once powered downtown industry, had outlived its original purpose but continued to block fish passage; removing the roughly eight-foot structure reconnected about 40 miles of upstream habitat and was expected to benefit 16 fish species and improve movement and genetic mixing among about 50 species, including the threatened or endangered greater redhorse, longnose dace and northern brook lamprey.In Montana, removal of the more than century-old Rattlesnake Creek Dam reconnected the Rattlesnake Wilderness with the Clark Fork River, while restoration plans included removing other structures, restoring about 1,000 feet of stream channel and creating five acres of wetland and floodplain habitat. On Washington’s Pilchuck River, two diversion dams were removed by the Tulalip Tribes and City of Snohomish, opening more than 36 miles of upstream habitat for Chinook, coho, chum and pink salmon, steelhead, bull trout, cutthroat trout and other species, while also reducing dam-failure risks and improving recreational opportunities.The 69 dam removals in 2020 were small compared with major US dams, but together they reconnected 624 miles of river. They restored fish passage in some areas while removing redundant or unsafe infrastructure in others.The wider debate includes larger proposals, such as Congressman Mike Simpson’s 2021 plan to remove four lower Snake River dams as part of a broader strategy involving salmon, energy, agriculture and regional infrastructure.
Article Summary: In 2020, 69 dams were removed across 23 states, reopening hundreds of miles of waterways that had been blocked for decades. Some structures had outlived the purpose for which they were built, while others had become expensive to maintain or posed growing safety concerns. For fish and wildlife, the changes could be significant, restoring access to stretches of river that had long been cut off.

Article Title: Jaws director Steven Spielberg protected 7.46 East Hampton acres with conservation easements in 2011; all 3 marsh and forest parcels are closed to development
Article Text:
An aerial view of East Hampton, New York, where Steven Spielberg placed conservation easements on three properties in 2011 | Wikimedia Commons

An aerial view of East Hampton, New York, where Steven Spielberg placed conservation easements on three properties in 2011 | Wikimedia Commons

Three separate pieces of land

Spielberg lived across the water

The restrictions went beyond construction

Georgica Beach | Wikimedia Commons

What did the easement change?

Steven Spielberg placed conservation easements on three properties in East Hampton Village in 2011, which permanently protected 7.46 acres from development. The land sits around Georgica Cove and contains brackish tidal marsh, maritime forest, old field and shrubland.The parcels were held through a Spielberg family subsidiary called the S.A.M. Trust. The Peconic Land Trust received the conservation easements, while the Village of East Hampton approved the transaction. The three properties measure 2.45, 2.65 and 2.36 acres respectively, according to the Peconic Land Trust's 2011 newsletter The properties are located around Chauncey Close and Cove Hollow Farm Road near Georgica Cove. Two of the parcels are next to one another, while the third lies across a small road. The conservation easements placed permanent restrictions on what could be done with the land, and the Peconic Land Trust said the easements prohibited vegetative screening and landscaping except when such work was needed to manage or improve natural habitat or prevent a public hazard.The land trust described the properties as remnants of the former Cove Hollow Farm, whose habitats included brackish tidal marsh and successional maritime forest, along with old fields and shrubland.The organization said the protected areas contributed to the health of Georgica Cove and Georgica Pond and provided habitat for mammals, birds, turtles and other wetland species.Spielberg's family home, Quelle Farm, was on Apaquogue Road across the water from the three parcels. A December 2011 report in The East Hampton Star said Spielberg had donated the conservation easements through the S.A.M. Trust to the Peconic Land Trust. It reported that the three parcels were located in the Cove Hollow Farm neighborhood at the intersection of Chauncey Close and Ruxton Road. The East Hampton Village Board had approved the transaction at a meeting that month, with village administrator Larry Cantwell saying that the approval recognized that the easement and gift were consistent with village policies for preserving natural resources. Spielberg did not simply hand the parcels over to a public agency; instead, the conservation easements placed legally binding restrictions on development while the land remained under private ownership.The 7.46 acres were protected from development but the restrictions extended further, as seen by the Peconic Land Trust's account, which says that landscaping was also prohibited except where it served a conservation purpose or addressed a public hazard. The parcels were valuable waterfront land, which is why that matters. The easements preserved the existing ecological communities rather than allowing the properties to be cleared or landscaped as conventional residential lots.The land trust specifically linked the protection to Georgica Cove and Georgica Pond, and its 2011 publication said the easements would help protect habitat used by numerous mammals, birds, turtles and other wetland species. The village's involvement also gave the arrangement a local planning dimension. The transaction was approved not as a public acquisition of a park, but as a conservation measure consistent with East Hampton's policies on natural resources.The Peconic Land Trust's records identify the three conservation easements as covering 7.46 acres of natural habitat, and the restrictions were mainly designed to remain with the properties rather than expire when ownership changed. The three parcels needed to be preserved as they kept a section of tidal marsh, forest, old field and shrubland from being converted into a more developed residential landscape.Spielberg's role was tied to the land through the S.A.M. Trust rather than through a public park created in his name, and the conservation easements instead provided a legal mechanism to keep the three parcels undeveloped while maintaining their existing habitat. The Peconic Land Trust continues to describe conservation easements as a way of permanently protecting natural lands while ownership can remain private.
Article Summary: Spielberg placed conservation easements on three properties in East Hampton Village in 2011, which permanently protected 7.46 acres from development. The three properties measure 2.45, 2.65 and 2.36 acres respectively. Spielberg's family home, Quelle Farm, was on Apaquogue Road across the water from the three parcels.

Article Title: At 22, Theodore Roosevelt bought 155 acres in Oyster Bay; today, Sagamore Hill is a National Historic Site open to visitors
Article Text:
The view of Theodore Roosevelt's home at the Sagamore Hill National Historic Site. Credits: NPS

The journey from a 155-acre purchase to Sagamore Hill

A farm woven into the family life

The view of Theodore Roosevelt's home at the Sagamore Hill National Historic Site. Credits: Wikimedia Commons

Transformation from Roosevelt home to National Historic Site

At 22, Theodore Roosevelt, who was the 26th President of the United States, purchased 155 acres in the Oyster Bay Cove area of Long Island. He bought the land for $30,000 and set in motion the creation of a home that would become Sagamore Hill. Eventually, the property was a reflection of several chapters of Roosevelt’s life: it was his family home, a working farm and, during his presidency, a summer base for conducting national affairs. Today, the estate is preserved as Sagamore Hill National Historic Site. The site does not still operate as a commercial farm, though. Instead, it is now preserved and interpreted for visitors.Reports suggest that Roosevelt had known Oyster Bay since he was a child, as he used to visit the Long Island area with his family during summer vacations in the 1870s. According to the National Park Service , he became attached to its natural setting and enjoyed activities such as hiking, rowing, swimming and riding. After finishing college, Roosevelt decided to purchase land in Oyster Bay, as he believed it to be the right place to settle and raise a family. He therefore bought farmland in Cove Neck and envisioned a substantial home on the property.In 1884, Roosevelt reportedly hired New York City architects Lamb and Rich to design a large Queen Anne-style residence, and the construction of the same began later that year. The plan, however, faced a major interruption when Roosevelt’s wife, Alice Hathaway Lee Roosevelt, died in February 1884, just two days after giving birth to their daughter, who was also named Alice.The house was eventually completed in 1885 by John A. Wood and Son at the cost of $16,975 after Roosevelt decided to proceed with the construction. He named the house Sagamore Hill.In 1886, Roosevelt became acquainted with Edith Kermit Carow, and the two got married later that year. Historical records show that Theodore and Edith took up full-time residence at Sagamore Hill in 1887, and would raise a total of six children, including his eldest daughter Alice, making the estate the centre of the Roosevelt family’s life for the following decades.Roosevelt had also dedicated 47 acres of the land to farmland, and the first buildings erected on the property were a stable and lodge that were constructed before the main house was built. The farmland included pasture and cultivated land that used to support the household. As per the federal organisation’s records, cows, chickens, turkeys and pigs were among the animals kept on the farm, while workers cultivated hay and straw alongside maintaining fruit and vegetable groves.Instead of being an ornamental feature on the estate, the agricultural work was part of the household’s daily routine. Edith Roosevelt managed most of the property alongside the household responsibilities. NPS noted in their account that she would often send Roosevelt to help the farmhands bring in hay when she thought he was working too hard. Meanwhile, Roosevelt allegedly enjoyed the physical labour and reportedly even insisted the farm manager put his name on the time sheets so he could receive the daily wage after spending a day working alongside the employees.The farm’s size and production varied as Roosevelt bought and sold portions of the surrounding property to relatives between 1884 and 1906. The NPS currently describes the Sagamore Hill National Historic Site as protecting approximately 83 acres of the historic estate and its natural surroundings.The farm also accommodated Roosevelt’s growing political career. After becoming president in 1901, Roosevelt wanted to escape Washington’s summer heat and moved his office to Sagamore Hill during the warmer months. Therefore, from 1902 through 1908, the estate was considered his Summer White House for seven summers during his presidency, which eventually ended in 1909.Despite the presidential role, the property’s domestic character was left intact, as it continued to function as the Roosevelt family home while also hosting political meetings and esteemed guests. NPS noted that visitors staying with the Roosevelts could enjoy meals supplied in part by produce from the farm.Roosevelt remained at Sagamore Hill until his death on 6 January 1919, while Edith continued living there until her death in 1948. Theodore Roosevelt Jr., their eldest son, later acquired four acres from Edith in 1938 and built a house known as Old Orchard in an area that had once been the property’s apple orchard. This indicates that the property’s later history was not simply the preservation of one unchanged presidential residence, but the continuation of a family landscape that had evolved over generations.The federal organisation says that Sagamore Hill National Historic Site was officially authorised by Congress on July 25, 1962, with the land formally transferring to the government the following year. The preserved property now includes Roosevelt’s home and the surrounding landscape, allowing visitors to experience the setting in which the former president lived from the late 19th century until his death in the early 20th century.

He hired New York City architects Lamb and Rich to design a large Queen Anne-style residence. The house was eventually completed in 1885 by John A.
