Article Title: A retired North Carolina repairman built giant wind-powered sculptures from scrap; after 30 were moved downtown, the park drew 194,300 visitors and generated $5.3 million in regional sales
Article Text:
Simpson used salvaged road signs, bicycle parts and scrap metal to create towering structures that moved with the wind.

From farm collection to downtown park

Property values rose around the park

Kids enjoy the open space of the park during an event.

Visitor numbers have grown

Simpson’s work lives on

Vollis Simpson spent much of his life repairing farm machinery in Wilson County, North Carolina. After retiring, he began building huge wind-powered sculptures on his farm using discarded materials. What started as a hobby soon grew into a collection that drew visitors from across the country.Simpson, a self-taught folk artist, began building the monumental kinetic sculptures in his 60s. According to the Vollis Simpson Whirligig Park & Museum, he used salvaged road signs, bicycle parts and scrap metal to create towering structures that moved with the wind. The works later became recognised as examples of American Folk Art.The sculptures first stood on Simpson’s farm in Lucama, about 11 miles outside Wilson. As word spread, especially after the rise of the internet, visitors began travelling to see them. The farm eventually became Wilson County’s top tourist destination, according to a 2020 economic impact report prepared for the City of Wilson.But Simpson grew older and the sculptures began to deteriorate. The Wilson community then worked to preserve his creations and bring them into the city.The result was the Vollis Simpson Whirligig Park, a roughly two-acre public art park in downtown Wilson that opened in November 2017.The park was created through a public-private partnership involving the City of Wilson and the nonprofit Vollis Simpson Whirligig Park and Museum. It now contains 30 restored large-scale kinetic sculptures.The move was a major undertaking, involving the conservation and installation of the sculptures at the new downtown site. The aim was not only to preserve Simpson’s work but also to create a public gathering space and encourage activity in downtown Wilson.That effort appears to have had a measurable economic effect. A 2020 economic impact study found that, during the park’s early years, visitors from outside the region generated about $1.7 million in spending in Wilson County annually. After accounting for the wider economic ripple effects, tourism linked to the park generated about $752,000 in annual earnings and supported 28 full-time jobs.The study also examined property values in an area containing about 340 parcels around the park. In 2009, before the park project was announced, properties in the study area had a combined assessed value of about $49.8 million. By 2019, that figure had reached $67.7 million, a 36% increase.The report compared that rise with property values across Wilson. The total assessed value within the city remained almost unchanged during the same period. The park area therefore had gained more than $17.9 million in assessed value over the 10-year period.Commercial activity also increased. Property owners and real estate professionals interviewed for the report described the park as a major asset and a “draw” for downtown.One property owner said they “would not have done” their first redevelopment project without the positive announcements around the Whirligig Park and nearby Whirligig Station.The report said the park and other downtown investments helped create what one interviewee called a “destination”, while another described the change as going from “dead to active”.The park’s visitor numbers have continued to grow since the period covered by the 2020 study. According to the Whirligig Park’s current figures, about 194,300 people visited the park in 2024, including roughly 92,550 visitors from outside the region.The park says its annual economic impact has now reached $5.3 million in total regional sales, with an annual income impact of $1.9 million and 42 jobs supported.In 2019, regular visitation was estimated at about 90 people a day, or nearly 32,850 visitors for the year. The study also found that visitors from outside Wilson County were an important source of new spending because their money was considered new economic activity for the county.Simpson died in 2013, four years before the park opened. But the sculptures he built from scrap continue to form the centrepiece of downtown Wilson.The park now presents 30 of his restored works in one location, allowing visitors to see the machines that once stood on his farm. The organisation behind the park continues to operate it through its partnership with the City of Wilson.
Article Summary: Vollis Simpson spent much of his life repairing farm machinery in Wilson County, North Carolina. After retiring, he began building huge wind-powered sculptures on his farm using discarded materials. What started as a hobby soon grew into a collection that drew visitors from across the country. Simpson died in 2013, four years before the park opened.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Beyoncé: “Don't try to lessen yourself...” - a powerful lesson on self-belief and authenticity
Article Text:
Quote of the Day by Beyoncé

Quote of the day by Beyoncé

“Don't try to lessen yourself for the world; let the world catch up to you.”

Where this line actually comes from

What the quote actually means

Why this idea still matters today

Self-belief does not mean rejecting criticism

The world may need time to understand something new

Beyoncé’s career gives the words added weight

Confidence still has to be backed by work

Other memorable quotes by Beyoncé

“The world will respect you as much as you respect yourself.”

“You can decide what success looks like for yourself.”

“I have learnt that my voice is clearer when I am still.”

“I push them and I push myself. It’s just who I am.”

How to apply this quote in daily life

Why these words still resonate

There is a difference between adapting to the world and reducing yourself to fit it. Beyoncé’s widely shared advice, “Don't try to lessen yourself for the world; let the world catch up to you,” speaks directly to that tension. On the surface, it sounds like confidence: do not become smaller simply because other people are not ready for what you bring. Beneath that is a demanding idea about patience, self-knowledge and the courage to keep developing work or an identity that may not receive immediate approval. Coming from an artist whose career has repeatedly tested the boundaries of genre and popular expectation, the line carries particular weight. It asks a difficult question: when the world does not immediately understand you, should you change yourself—or give it time to understand?The quote is often circulated online as a standalone Beyoncé saying, but its clearest documented context comes through Chloe and Halle Bailey, the sister duo Beyoncé mentored and signed to Parkwood Entertainment. In a 2017 interview discussed by Essence, the sisters described Beyoncé as encouraging them to remain true to themselves, with Chloe recalling her advice: “Don't try to lessen yourself for the world; let the world catch up to you. ” Around the same period, Halle told W Magazine that Beyoncé’s message was to let the world catch up rather than “dumb” their music down, after the young artists had heard that their work might be too complex for an average listener.A 2018 Nylon profile recorded a closely related version of the advice. The available reporting therefore places the line in the context of Beyoncé mentoring younger artists and protecting their creative individuality, rather than in a public speech or published essay. That matters because the sentence was not simply abstract encouragement; it was advice about what to do when originality creates pressure to become more conventional.The key word in the quote is “lessen.” Beyoncé is not saying that people should refuse criticism, reject growth or assume that every idea they have is ahead of its time. She is warning against a different impulse: deliberately reducing your ability, ambition, identity or creative instincts simply to become easier for others to accept. “Let the world catch up” introduces patience into the idea. Recognition does not always arrive at the same moment as originality. A student may have an unconventional career goal, an artist may create work that does not fit familiar categories, or an employee may approach a problem differently from the accepted method. The quote suggests that unfamiliarity is not, by itself, evidence that something is wrong. The harder task is learning to distinguish useful feedback, which can improve you, from pressure that merely asks you to become less distinctive.That distinction is especially relevant in a culture shaped by algorithms, trends and instant reaction. Social media can reward recognisable formats quickly, while unusual work may need more time to find an audience. The same pressure appears at work and in education, where people can feel pushed to sound, dress, create or behave in ways that already seem acceptable. Beyoncé’s line offers a useful counterweight: immediate approval should not become the only test of value. Adapting a presentation, learning from criticism or improving a skill can be sensible; erasing the quality that makes the work yours is different. The challenge is to remain flexible about method without becoming uncertain about identity.Refusing to make yourself smaller should not be confused with believing you are beyond correction. Healthy self-belief can coexist with rigorous self-editing and difficult feedback. Beyoncé has spoken about being highly critical of her work and pushing herself creatively, while also insisting that she must ultimately make her own decisions. That combination changes the meaning of the quote. The point is not “ignore everyone. ” It is to know which compromises improve the work and which remove the quality that made it worth doing.New ideas often look less strange after people have had time to encounter them. Music, fashion, technology and workplace habits can move from unfamiliar to mainstream once audiences understand their value. That does not make every unconventional idea successful, but it explains why instant acceptance can be a poor measure of potential. Sometimes resistance calls for revision; at other times, it calls for consistency long enough for understanding to catch up.Beyoncé’s career gives the advice added weight. Her work has crossed music, visual storytelling and business ownership, while projects such as Cowboy Carter challenged familiar genre boundaries. At the 2025 Grammys, the album won Album of the Year and Best Country Album, making Beyoncé the first Black woman to win the latter category. She now holds 35 Grammys, the most of any artist.Self-belief becomes convincing only when supported by work. In her 2020 “Dear Class of 2020” address, Beyoncé paired authenticity with effort, failure, accountability and respect. That puts an important limit on the quote: asking the world to catch up is not permission to stand still. It means developing the discipline and skill that make confidence more than a pose.Start by noticing the moments when you make yourself smaller before anyone has asked you to. You may stay quiet in a meeting despite having a useful idea, hide an ambitious goal because friends may find it unrealistic, or simplify creative work because it does not resemble what is popular. Ask whether the change improves what you are doing or merely makes it safer and more familiar. Listen seriously to criticism and revise when it identifies a real weakness. But if the only objection is that your direction is unusual, give it enough time and work to prove itself. The aim is not to resist the world; it is to stop confusing acceptance with worth.The lasting appeal of Beyoncé’s words lies in a choice most people face: belonging quickly or remaining recognisably themselves. The pressure may appear in a career, classroom, relationship or creative pursuit, and it rarely arrives as a direct demand to become smaller. More often, it appears as an invitation to be quieter, safer or more predictable. “Let the world catch up to you” does not guarantee that others will agree or applaud. Instead, it offers permission to let recognition take time while continuing to improve and trust what is genuinely yours. The goal is not to be different for its own sake, but to avoid abandoning something valuable simply because others have not learned how to see it.
Article Summary: Beyoncé’s widely shared advice, “Don't try to lessen yourself for the world; let the world catch up to you,” speaks directly to that tension. On the surface, it sounds like confidence: do not become smaller simply because other people are not ready for what you bring. Beneath that is a demanding idea about patience, self-knowledge and the courage to keep developing work that may not receive immediate approval.

Article Title: South Florida teens are using pizza and technology to fight hunger in America: Delivered 25,000 slices to families in need
Article Text:
Through the platform, users can select a nearby restaurant or grocery store and direct pizzas and other commodities to a charity in the same area.

A South Florida teen and her brother are using pizza and technology to fight hunger in the country. Aashrita Kaza and her brother Anish have developed Pizza for a Purpose in Florida, an app that connects donors, pizzerias and local organisations. According to a report published by Good News Network, the platform started in 2024 and has already facilitated the donation of 25,000 slices of pizza to families facing food insecurity, including residents of Broward County.The idea came after the siblings saw food insecurity firsthand. The 13-year-old and her brother were volunteering at local places when they noticed families were in line for food and those in the queue included not only adults but also young children their age. "It just shocked us because we didn't think there were kids our age who needed food," said Aashrita.The duo realised that technology could bridge the gap between those wishing to donate food and the organisation needing to receive it. Instead of requiring donors to buy the food, pick up the order and find an organisation to deliver it, Pizza for Purpose streamlines the process while still achieving the goal.Through the platform, users can select a nearby restaurant or grocery store and direct pizzas and other commodities to a charity in the same area.The app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play Store."The reaction really warms our hearts, their faces just light up the second they get the pizza," said co-founder Aashrita. "It's very rewarding because it makes everything we do worth it."One of their partners, The Pantry of Broward, serves more than 600 people each month. "So, to be able to receive fresh, hot pizzas and hand-deliver them directly to our clients is just a blessing. The smiles on their faces, it's very rewarding, whether it's a grandparent taking it home to their grandkids, or whether it's just a senior who having a pizza for dinner is a luxury item," The Pantry of Broward COO Warren Lubow said to CBS News.By August 2026, this model had already contributed to the distribution of 25,000 slices. An estimated 47.9 million people lived in food-insecure households in US, according to data from the USDA Economic Research Service. According to Feeding America, roughly 14 million children experience hunger or food insecurity annually. In this context, the app made by the teens is making an immense impact in ensuring not every stomach goes hungry at night.Individuals can also use the Pizza for a Purpose app to make a donation, giving anyone a way to help provide a fresh meal to a family in need.The teens have also started Dhanam Foundation, inspired by the Sanskrit word 'Dhanam', which embodies the spirit of compassion and generosity and continues their initiative beyond the app.The story of Aashrita and Anish illustrates how a volunteering experience can uncover issues that are not always visible to those outside assistance institutions
Article Summary: A South Florida teen and her brother are using pizza and technology to fight hunger in the country. Pizza for a Purpose is an app that connects donors, pizzerias and local organisations. The platform started in 2024 and has already facilitated the donation of 25,000 slices of pizza to families facing food insecurity.

Article Title: In 2011, Illinois businessman Jim Bolin built a record-breaking wind chime to draw travelers into Casey; 15 years later, his project had grown to 21 giant objects and 12 Guinness records
Article Text:
Bolin, the creator of “Big Things in a Small Town”, died in January 2026 (Guinness world records photos)

Wind chime changed Casey

Pitchforks, golf tees, mailboxes and rocking chairs are among the town’s six-plus record-holding attractions.

21 giant objects

Records changed town

'Absolute legend'

A small Illinois town found a new way to attract visitors when businessman Jim Bolin built a giant wind chime. Over the years, businessman Bolin turned that idea into a collection of oversized everyday objects that made Casey known for its unusual attractions.Bolin, the creator of 'Big Things in a Small Town', died in January 2026 after sustaining injuries during a snowmobile trip, according to Guinness World Records . His company, Bolin Enterprises, described him as a man with 'unwavering devotion to his family' and 'genuine friendship to all'.Bolin’s project had started years earlier when Casey was struggling to attract visitors. The town, located off Interstate 70 between Effingham and Terre Haute, Indiana, was like many other small communities in the area. Bolin and his family wanted to open a tea shop, but there were not enough people stopping in the town.In 2012, Bolin built what was described as the world’s largest wind chime. The idea was inspired by memories of listening to his grandmother’s wind chime on her porch. His experience in the pipeline construction business also meant he already had access to some of the parts needed for the project.The wind chime became the starting point for something much larger.Casey residents and leaders followed the idea and began adding more oversized objects to the town.The attractions included a giant pitchfork, golf tee, mailbox, rocking chair, golf club, barber’s pole, teeter-totter and other objects. Some were not record holders, but were still large enough to attract visitors.By 2019, NPR Illinois reported that the town had more than six attractions holding world records, while two others had already been surpassed. Another 10 attractions were large but did not hold records.Deb Bohannon, who helped market tourism in Casey, said the project had helped rejuvenate the community, which had around 3,000 residents at the time. She said the town had seen more than 1,500 people in a single weekend.Guinness World Records later documented the scale of Bolin’s work. Over about 15 years, he collected 12 Guinness World Records titles for 21 different objects.Among them was the largest wind chime, measuring 49 feet (14.94 metres) tall. The project also included the longest seesaw or teeter-totter, measuring 82 feet (25.01 metres), and the largest rocking chair, which stood 56 feet 1 inch (17.09 metres) tall.The objects were not simply large decorations. Many of them were designed to work or allow visitors to interact with them.The giant wind chime can clang when the wind moves through it. Visitors can climb inside the enormous pair of clogs. The giant mailbox has a staircase inside, allowing people to reach the box and see a mail history museum.The mailbox also has a giant flag that can be raised and lowered when mail is deposited. These features were created to make the objects part of the visitor experience rather than simply things to look at.The impact of the project was visible in the attention Casey received from visitors and the media. Photographs and videos of its oversized objects spread, while the Guinness World Records titles gave the town another reason to attract tourists.“These world records have just changed our town tremendously,” Bolin told Guinness World Records in 2016.Bohannon said Casey residents looked at what other towns were doing, then tried to adapt those ideas for their own community.“If you can get the community leaders together and say ok this is where we are at today and this is where we want to be tomorrow. Now how do we get there?” she said.She also stressed that the change did not happen immediately. “It didn't happen overnight,” Bohannon said. “It took one initiative and one person to start it. It took the whole community to back it.”Guinness World Records described Bolin as an “absolute legend”, a “genuine pleasure to work with” and the “King of the Big Stuff”.Guinness World Records Editor-in-Chief Craig Glenday also remembered the businessman after his death.“I always loved seeing how his record-breaking builds brought so much joy to the world!” Glenday said. “Jim showed us all how just one person can make a difference. In his case, a big difference.”
Article Summary: Businessman Jim Bolin built the world's largest wind chime in Casey, Illinois. The idea was inspired by memories of listening to his grandmother's chime. Over 15 years, Bolin collected 12 Guinness World Records titles for 21 different objects. The project also included the longest seesaw or teeter-totter and the largest rocking chair.

Article Title: Play, deport, repeat: Trump launches arcade-style immigration games
Article Text:
The website, unveiled on Thursday, gives a “MAGA” twist to familiar games such as Snake and Tetris. It was presented by the White House as a new way to promote Trump’s policies through entertainment and social media.

US President Donald Trump has taken a soft power approach to his deportation agenda. The White House has launched an online gaming website featuring arcade-style games that let players deport migrants and build a border wall, as his administration intensifies its crackdown on undocumented immigration.The website, unveiled on Thursday, gives a “MAGA” twist to familiar games such as Snake and Tetris. It was presented by the White House as a new way to promote Trump’s policies through entertainment and social media.In a series of posts shared on X, the White House teased a bunch of deportation themed games that were inspired by some of the most popular arcade games.It teased the launch of the website by a video featuring a "make America great again” logo styled after the branding of video game maker Sega. The video then goes on to show snippets of gameplay from various games. The White House promoted the games on X with “CAN'T STOP WINNING. Build the wall. Deport. Fill a Trump Account,” the post said.One of the games, Rio Run, is based on Snake. It features a digital version of US border czar Tom Homan chasing migrants of different skin colours along the Rio Grande, which forms part of the US-Mexico border.Another game, Build the Wall, is modelled on Tetris. Players stack blocks to construct a border wall.Its instructions tell users to “Protect the border from the coming horde.”A third game asks players to collect nets and place them into so-called “Trump accounts”. These are investment accounts containing a $1,000 deposit for children born between 2025 and 2028.The White House said the games were designed to communicate the administration’s policies in a format that could reach a wider audience.“This administration is laser-focused on ways to innovate and tell the story of the President's many accomplishments in a way that resonates with every American,” the White House said in a statement to AFP, “This is an effort to further contrast between a culture of fun and winning and the dark socialist vision Democrats have for America.”The launch, however, drew swift criticism from rights groups, who accused the administration of turning the lives of migrants into entertainment.“Makes me sick. They've been playing games with people's lives for years, now they've made a video game of what they're doing,” Amerika Garcia Grewal, co-director of the Frontera Federation in Eagle Pass, Texas, told AFP.“There’s no attention paid to the quality of life for human beings, both those in their game or those in real life. We who live in the borderlands are US citizens and yet are treated with suspicion and violence,” she added.The game designers “have lost touch with what it means to be human and care for others.”Trump returned to power after campaigning on a promise to deport millions of undocumented migrants. Since taking office, his administration has introduced measures aimed at speeding up deportations and reducing illegal border crossings.The White House has also frequently used social media stunts and provocative online content to promote Trump’s agenda and mock his political opponents.The gaming campaign comes amid that broader push, with immigration enforcement remaining one of the administration’s central priorities.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump has taken a soft power approach to his deportation agenda. The website, unveiled on Thursday, gives a “MAGA’ twist to familiar games such as Snake and Tetris. It was presented by the White House as a new way to promote Trump’s policies.

Article Title: In 1973, a North Dakota couple bought a 4,800-acre ranch getting just 10 inches of rain a year; 53 years later, beavers are back and 270 acres are being restored to native grass
Article Text:
The projects helped to spread livestock more evenly and reduced pressure on sensitive riparian areas and improved water quality.

Water management restores wildlife

Building soil from the ground up

Making habitat for birds

A legacy of knowledge sharing

In one of North Dakota’s driest corners, where annual rainfall averages just 10 inches, John Lee and Ellen Njos have spent more than five decades showing that working land and conservation can go forward together. Since buying the 4,800-acre Coyote Creek Ranch near Rhame in Bowman County in 1973, the couple has gradually changed how they graze, water and manage their land. The family has now been awarded the 2026 North Dakota Leopold Conservation Award for their efforts, which recognize landowners who make exceptional contributions to soil health, water quality and wildlife habitat. The Njoses will receive the $10,000 in December, states Morning AgClips report. Survival on the ranch has often been a matter of doing something out of the ordinary. John Lee’s philosophy of conservation was taking shape when he joined his local soil conservation district board in 1986. So the district sent him to a holistic grazing course taught by Allan Savory. It opened his eyes to new ways of using fences and moving livestock to encourage grass growth and help soil absorb more water. He took those lessons home and began experimenting.One of the first decisions was to install cross-fencing, despite the skepticism of others in the ranching community. The results were impressive, showing that well managed grazing could improve both the landscape and the productivity of the ranch. The experience formed the bedrock for decades of experimentation and education.In a world in which water is scarce, controlling its movement and availability has been at the heart of the Njoses’ conservation work. The family developed water infrastructure, including buried pipelines, solar wells and strategically placed dams. The projects helped to spread livestock more evenly and reduced pressure on sensitive riparian areas and improved water quality. They also created an unexpected ecological benefit: beavers returned to stretches of Coyote Creek. John Lee has maintained careful rainfall records for the two parcels of the ranch for 35 years, providing a long-term record of conditions in one of the most challenging environments in the region.The family’s conservation work isn’t just about grazing. Decades ago, John Lee planted strips of tall wheatgrass across fields to help fight wind erosion. More recently, the family adopted bale grazing as a strategy to add organic matter and carbon to nutrient-poor soils, and to reduce machinery use, fuel consumption and emissions. Cover crops are also planted on degraded cropland. The different plantings help rebuild soil structure, support microbial activity, reduce erosion, and provide additional forage for cattle and wildlife.The Njoses have also incorporated wildlife conservation into their working ranch approach. They have worked with the Bird Conservancy of the Rockies, Ducks Unlimited, North Dakota Game & Fish and Audubon on bird inventories, migration research and grassland bird capture and tagging. The family is restoring 270 acres with a variety of native grasses and forbs through Audubon’s Conservation Forage Program. Their participation in the third-party verified Bird Friendly Beef program suggests that their grazing practices are intended to benefit grassland bird populations. The family has also been instrumental in assembling landowners in sage grouse management to develop workable conservation strategies benefiting wildlife and ranching.Today John Lee and Ellen farm with their daughter Angie and her husband, Luke Rodakowski. Their son Chad, who runs a nearby ranch, takes a similar approach to conservation. John Lee's influence reaches well beyond his own acreage. He has worked with other ranchers over the years, helped start the North Dakota Grazing Lands Coalition and been involved in regional and national conservation efforts. The Leopold Conservation Award is given by the Sand County Foundation and American Farmland Trust in conjunction with North Dakota agricultural and conservation groups to honor landowners whose practices reflect a long-term commitment to land health. At Coyote Creek Ranch, that commitment has been measured not just in acres or infrastructure, but in healthier grass, improved water management, returning wildlife, and a willingness to share hard-earned lessons with the next generation of land stewards.
Article Summary: John Lee and Ellen Njos have spent more than five decades showing that working land and conservation can go forward together. Couple has gradually changed how they graze, water and manage their land. The family has now been awarded the 2026 North Dakota Leopold Conservation Award for their efforts.

Article Title: 3 California hikers trusted AI to plan Mount Shasta climb; 8-hour trek became a 16-hour ordeal that left them injured, stranded overnight and ultimately rescued
Article Text:
Hikers and rescuers make their way down Mount Shasta after the group became stranded during their descent. / Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Office

California hikers began climb with an AI-assisted plan

They reached the summit seven hours after the turnaround time

Darkness, dead batteries and a wrong turn left them stranded

Rangers found them the next morning

Authorities warn against relying on AI in the backcountry

Three novice hikers from Roseville, California, were rescued from Mount Shasta after an attempted summit climb that they had planned with substantial help from Google's Gemini AI turned into a dangerous overnight ordeal. The three men expected their ascent to take about eight hours and carried food and water based partly on that plan. Instead, they reached the 14,179-foot summit at about 7 p.m. on Sunday, August 30, well beyond the recommended noon turnaround time. Their descent took place in darkness, and they eventually wandered off route into the Mud Creek Canyon drainage. One hiker injured his knee after a fall, their phone used for navigation lost power and the group spent the night without adequate food, water, warm clothing or emergency shelter before Forest Service climbing rangers reached them the next morning.The three men left the Clear Creek Trailhead on Mount Shasta's southeastern side on Saturday, August 29, and established a base camp at about 8,400 feet. According to the U.S. Forest Service and Siskiyou County Sheriff's Office accounts, the group were novice climbers and had used several digital sources while preparing for the trip, including Google's Gemini, YouTube and the AllTrails mapping application. Gemini was used for information about the route as well as decisions about what food and how much water to carry.The group planned around an approximately eight-hour climb and set off from their camp at about 3 a.m. on Sunday carrying daypacks. Authorities later said Gemini had advised them to take considerably less food and water than they ultimately needed.The climb took considerably longer than expected. The hikers did not reach the summit until approximately 7 p.m., even though climbers on Mount Shasta are advised to turn around by noon if they have not reached the summit. The rule is designed to leave sufficient daylight for the descent and reduce the risk of people becoming stranded. By reaching the summit roughly seven hours after that recommended turnaround point, the group began its return in darkness. The Forest Service said the climbers had been advised to turn around during the ascent, but they continued and eventually reached the summit. Their roughly eight-hour plan had effectively become a much longer undertaking before they even began the descent.About an hour after leaving the summit, the hikers contacted the Siskiyou County Sheriff's Office dispatch for directions, but they eventually wandered off the established route and into the Mud Creek Canyon drainage. They had been using AllTrails for navigation, but the phone running the application ran out of battery and a backup charger failed. The Forest Service said one member also had a Garmin watch, although the group primarily relied on visual navigation during the descent. At around 11,500 feet, one of the hikers fell and injured his knee. The group eventually stopped at about midnight in the steep drainage and spent the night there. They lacked enough food and water for an unexpected overnight stay and did not have adequate warm layers or emergency shelter.U.S. Forest Service climbing rangers reached the stranded hikers at about 9:30 a.m. on Monday, August 31. The rangers provided first aid to the injured climber as well as food and water for the group. Siskiyou County Search and Rescue volunteers were deployed to assist with the operation. Helicopter assistance was complicated by conditions at the higher elevations, with the Forest Service reporting difficulties with attempted helicopter hoists. The hikers therefore continued down the mountain with the climbing rangers. They eventually reached their base camp at about 3 p.m., where county search-and-rescue personnel helped escort them back towards the Clear Creek Trailhead. The hikers and rescuers returned without further incident.After the rescue, the hikers acknowledged that they had put too much faith in the technology. According to the Forest Service account, they said, “We relied too much on AI rather than our own critical thinking.” The Siskiyou County Sheriff's Office described the use of Gemini as a “critical misstep”, saying the hikers had been advised to bring far less food and water than their group required. Officials stressed, however, that the rescue resulted from a combination of problems rather than a single AI-generated error. The group continued beyond the recommended turnaround time, descended after dark, lost its primary navigation method, went off route and had insufficient supplies for an unexpected night on the mountain. Authorities now advise climbers to contact the Mount Shasta Ranger Station before a trip, use established local information, carry multiple navigation methods including a paper map, regularly verify their position and prepare for an unplanned overnight stay. The sheriff's office specifically advises climbers who have not reached the summit by noon to turn around.
Article Summary: Three novice hikers from Roseville, California, were rescued from Mount Shasta after an attempted summit climb that they had planned with substantial help from Google's Gemini AI turned into a dangerous overnight ordeal. The three men expected their ascent to take about eight hours and carried food and water based partly on that plan. Instead, they reached the 14,179-foot summit at about 7 p.m. on Sunday, August 30, well beyond the recommended noon turnaround time. Their descent took place in darkness, and they eventually wandered off route into the Mud Creek Canyon drainage. One hiker injured his knee after a fall

Article Title: An 1877 New Jersey house has served as a museum since 1924; after 102 years, a $1.5 million restoration is reviving its hidden 19th-century floors and preparing it to reopen
Article Text:
A museum hidden inside a historic home

The biggest surprise was underneath the carpet

Even the windows had been frozen in time

Behind the old walls, a modern museum is taking shape

A collection spanning centuries

After more than a century as the home of the Hopewell Museum, a nearly 150-year-old house in Hopewell, New Jersey, is undergoing a $1.5 million restoration designed to preserve its historic character while preparing it for the future. According to a report in the Hopewell Express, the museum is now in the third phase of its multiyear “Reimagination” project at 28 E. Broad St. The work is restoring original features, including historic floors, windows and plasterwork, while adding modern systems to better protect the museum’s collections. The museum is expected to reopen in December 2026. The house was built in 1877 as the residence of Randolph Stout. As documented by the Hopewell Valley History Project, it became the home of the combined Hopewell library and museum in 1924, beginning a relationship with the institution that has lasted more than a century. A February report by Community News also detailed the third phase of the project, including interior restoration and upgrades to the building’s museum systems.The three-story brownstone was built in the Second Empire style, recognizable by its Mansard roof and projecting front bays.Before becoming a museum, it passed from the Stout family to Hugh A. Smith, who purchased it in 1906.The museum’s own history goes back to 1922, when the Hopewell Free Public Library and Museum Funding and Building Association was incorporated. The effort was prompted in part by a collection of antiques donated by Sarah D. Stout. Two years later, the Stout house was acquired for use by the library and museum. The library eventually moved elsewhere, leaving the building solely to the museum in the 1960s. But by 2018, decades of wear had become increasingly difficult to ignore. Floors, windows, pathways and mechanical systems all needed attention, leading to the larger restoration effort now underway.One of the most intriguing discoveries came in 2021, when sections of the building’s old carpet were pulled back. Underneath was an ornate hardwood inlay.As more carpet was removed, additional 19th-century parquet flooring emerged across the building. The floors have since been cleaned, coated and buffed, allowing their geometric patterns to become part of the restored museum interior. The discovery is particularly fitting for a museum whose building is itself an important part of its history.Restoring the windows proved to be another painstaking job. The museum’s 13 double-hung windows had been sealed, nailed or otherwise immobilised over the years. Their original hardware and chains had also been painted over.Restoration specialist Chris Fullan of Forever Hung Windows in Pennsylvania dismantled the windows and repaired their historic components, including the mortise-and-tenon sashes and old hardware. The original wavy glass was carefully reset before the windows were returned to their places. Rather than making the house look brand new, workers have also preserved elements that reveal its age.Plaster walls and three fireplaces were restored, while some old cracks and irregularities were intentionally retained. On the third floor, new plaster was shaped around existing walls and alcoves instead of flattening away the building’s historic character.The $1.5 million third phase is not simply cosmetic. The project includes new electrical and plumbing systems, upgraded heating and air conditioning, improved climate control and museum-quality lighting. Old knob-and-tube wiring discovered inside the walls is being replaced with modern electrical infrastructure.New LED and track lighting will allow exhibits to be illuminated differently depending on whether they contain artifacts, photographs, maps or other materials. The museum is also being made more accessible, including an ADA-compliant lift providing first-floor access through the west entrance.The renovated galleries will continue to showcase the history of Hopewell and the surrounding valley. The museum holds nearly 13,000 objects and artifacts, including Native American materials, tools, farm implements, furniture, textiles, china and glassware, photographs, maps, documents, Civil War artifacts and genealogical material.The first exhibition planned for the renovated galleries will bring objects from the collection together around a Hopewell Valley theme. The museum is currently closed to regular visitors but continues to offer scheduled research appointments from its temporary office at 43 Railroad Place. Its official website lists the reopening as late 2026, while the August 31 local report gives December as the expected target.When the doors finally reopen, visitors will see more than newly arranged exhibits. They will walk across floors laid down in the 19th century, look through painstakingly restored windows and move through rooms where traces of the old house have deliberately been left visible. After 102 years as a museum home, the building is becoming part of the exhibition all over again.
Article Summary: The Hopewell Museum in New Jersey is undergoing a $1.5 million restoration. It is restoring original features, including historic floors, windows and plasterwork, while adding modern systems to better protect the museum's collections. The museum is expected to reopen in December 2026.

Article Title: Texas ‘Killing Fields’: Man gets 20 years in teen’s death, first conviction tied to 4 women found at one site
Article Text:
Tim Miller, father of Laura Miller, speaks outside of the courtroom after James Dolphs Elmore Jr. was found guilty of manslaughter in Texas. (Photo: AP)

How did a decades-old case reach a jury?

Why did one field become central to the mystery?

What happened to the man authorities had focused on?

Why do most ‘Texas Killing Fields’ deaths remain unsolved?

A Texas man has been sentenced to the maximum 20 years in prison over the death of 16-year-old Laura Miller, whose remains were among those found in an area southeast of Houston where more than 30 girls and young women have turned up dead since the 1970s.The stretch around Interstate 45 became known as the “Texas Killing Fields” as bodies continued to be discovered over several decades and many of the deaths remained unsolved. James Dolphs Elmore Jr.'s conviction is the first linked to any of four women whose remains were found at one field off Calder Road in League City between 1984 and 1991.A Galveston County jury sentenced Elmore, 61, on Thursday, a day after finding him guilty of manslaughter in Miller's death. Prosecutors said he prepared cocaine that his longtime friend Clyde Hedrick administered to her.The Associated Press reported that Elmore approached Miller's father, Tim Miller, several years ago and told him he had been present when Laura died. The two men later met dozens of times.Elmore first contacted Tim Miller in 2022, nearly four decades after Laura disappeared. The two men met repeatedly, and Miller filmed some of their encounters, including visits to places linked to his daughter's death.Miller had spent years trying to find answers about Laura. After becoming frustrated with authorities during the search for his daughter, he founded Texas EquuSearch, a nonprofit that helps locate missing people.The Houston Chronicle reported that Miller paid Elmore about $33,000 over four years while seeking information that could help authorities build a case against Hedrick. Elmore also spoke to police about what he said happened on the night Laura died and said he had helped move her body to the Calder Road field.Prosecutors said Elmore prepared the cocaine and handed it to Hedrick, who administered it to Laura.Defence attorney Bill Agnew denied that Elmore was responsible and said his client likely would have been called to testify had Hedrick lived.“Clyde killed himself, and once that happened you've got one guy standing,” Agnew told jurors.Jurors deliberated for about an hour before finding Elmore guilty. The following day, they took roughly 30 minutes to impose the maximum 20-year sentence sought by prosecutors.During the trial, Tim Miller directly confronted Elmore over his role in Laura's death. “You handed it to Clyde Hedrick. You handed it,” Miller told him.Laura disappeared in 1984. Her remains were found 17 months later, in 1986. Three other young women — Audrey Cook, Heidi Fye-Villareal and Donna Prudhomme — were also found at the Calder Road field between 1984 and 1991.The four deaths became part of the wider mystery associated with the Texas Killing Fields, a series of deaths and disappearances linked to the Interstate 45 corridor southeast of Houston.Elmore is the first person convicted in connection with any of the four Calder Road women. His conviction does not resolve who was responsible for the other three deaths.Authorities had also focused on Hedrick in connection with the four Calder Road deaths.In March, prosecutors said they planned to seek grand jury indictments against him over the deaths. Hedrick died by suicide before the cases could be presented.He had previously been convicted of manslaughter in 2014 in the death of Ellen Beason. Beason disappeared in 1984 and was found dead the following year. Hedrick was released on parole in 2022.Elmore's conviction is not the first involving the wider Texas Killing Fields cases. In 2022, Oklahoma death row inmate William Reece pleaded guilty in Texas to murdering Laura Smither, Jessica Cain and Kelli Cox. He received three life sentences.But most deaths associated with the Texas Killing Fields remain unsolved, and investigators believe more than one person may have been responsible.Kenneth Cusick, who was appointed Galveston County district attorney last year, has said his office would take a harder look at the cases.
Article Summary: James Dolphs Elmore Jr. has been sentenced to the maximum 20 years in prison over the death of 16-year-old Laura Miller. Her remains were among those found in an area southeast of Houston where more than 30 girls and young women have turned up dead since the 1970s. The stretch around Interstate 45 became known as the ‘Texas Killing Fields’ as bodies continued to be discovered over several decades and many of the deaths remained unsolved.

Article Title: 25 Pakistani military personnel killed in Balochistan attacks, BLA claims
Article Text:
Balochistan: BLA claims 25 Pakistani military personnel killed in two attacks (Picture from X)

The Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) on Thursday claimed responsibility for two attacks in Pakistan’s Balochistan province, saying 25 Pakistani military personnel were killed and three military vehicles destroyed.According to The Balochistan Post, the BLA spokesperson said fighters targeted a military convoy at Ziarat Cross, attacking vehicles and destroying two of them, including a military truck.The militant group initially claimed that 18 personnel were killed in the attack, with the death toll later rising to 25.The BLA also released a one-minute-and-11-second video trailer through Hakkal, its official media channel, which it said showed footage from the Ziarat Cross attack.The footage purportedly shows armed fighters near burning Pakistani military vehicles, with bodies visible at the site and weapons being seized. The BLA said it would release the complete video later.In a separate operation in the Hajika area of Surab, the group’s Special Tactical Operations Squad (STOS) remotely detonated an explosives-laden vehicle, destroying a military vehicle and killing seven personnel, according to the BLA statement.
Article Summary: Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) claims responsibility for two attacks in Pakistan's Balochistan province. BLA says 25 Pakistani military personnel were killed and three military vehicles destroyed. The militant group also released a one-minute-and-11-second video trailer through Hakkal.

Article Title: ‘6ft by 8ft cell, brown drinking water’: What Imran Khan’s jail cell is like
Article Text:
The report said visitors have been barred and Khan has been confined to his cell for as much as 23 hours a day.

Former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan is being held in what has been described as harsh conditions at Rawalpindi’s Adiala Jail, with reports alleging prolonged isolation, limited access to reading material and restrictions on contact with his family.According to a report by The Times UK, Khan is being kept in a 6ft by 8ft cell typically used for prisoners on death row. The report said the 73-year-old has no reading material apart from the Quran and is being provided “soiled brown water” to drink.His sons, Sulaiman and Kasim Khan, have reportedly been unable to meet their father in person since 2022 and have at times been prevented from speaking to him by telephone for months. They have described his living conditions as inhumane “torture tactics”.The report said visitors have been barred and Khan has been confined to his cell for as much as 23 hours a day.The reported restrictions have also become the subject of repeated legal challenges by Khan’s family.His sister Uzma Khan filed a fresh contempt petition in the Supreme Court on Wednesday, alleging that authorities have failed to comply with an August 18 order concerning Khan’s access to his family.According to The Express Tribune, the petition names Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Adiala Jail Superintendent Sajid Baig, Punjab Inspector General of Prisons Mian Salik Jalal and other senior officials as respondents.The August 18 order had directed authorities to facilitate virtual communication between Khan and his sons and allow his sisters to meet him weekly. However, Uzma said she was denied a scheduled visit on Tuesday, while telephone communication between Khan and his sons has remained restricted since March.The petition also alleges that authorities failed to establish the infrastructure required for bi-weekly telephone calls with Sulaiman and Kasim.The latest dispute follows an earlier contempt petition over the alleged non-compliance with the Supreme Court’s direction to transfer Khan to Shifa International Hospital for medical evaluation. He was instead taken to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) on August 21 before being returned to Adiala Jail after doctors declared him “medically fit”. Authorities have cited security concerns for the decision.
Article Summary: Imran Khan is being held in what has been described as harsh conditions at Rawalpindi’s Adiala Jail. Reports allege prolonged isolation, limited access to reading material and restrictions on contact with his family. His sons, Sulaiman and Kasim Khan, have reportedly been unable to meet their father in person since 2022.

Article Title: Pakistan: Imran Khan's sister files fresh contempt plea over denied jail visits
Article Text: Former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan's sister Uzma Khan on Wednesday filed a fresh contempt of court petition in the Supreme Court, alleging non-enforcement of previous judicial directives issued by the country's apex court.In her petition, Uzma named several high-ranking officials, including Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif and Adiala (Rawalpindi Central Jail) Superintendent Sajid Baig, as respondents.According to the Express Tribune, the petition was filed after the Supreme Court's August 18 instructions, which mandated virtual communication between Imran Khan and his sons, alongside weekly access for his sisters, failed to materialise.The plea said that Uzma Khan was denied a scheduled visit on Tuesday and noted that audio communication with his sons has remained restricted since March.The petition alleged that authorities neglected to establish the necessary infrastructure enabling bi-weekly telephone calls with his sons, Kasim Khan and Sulaiman Khan, as previously ordered by the bench.Earlier, Uzma had filed another contempt application addressing government non-compliance regarding a separate instruction within the August 18 order, which directed that Imran Khan be moved to Shifa International Hospital for medical care.Under the original August 18 decision, the Supreme Court instructed that the former premier be transferred to Shifa International Hospital for clinical evaluation by a multidisciplinary medical panel while simultaneously granting visitation rights.Following the orders, authorities transferred Imran Khan to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) on August 21. He was, however, sent back to Adiala Jail shortly after medical personnel declared him to be "medically fit".Reacting to the developments, the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) lambasted prison administrators for barring relatives from seeing the party founder, characterising the restrictions as a flagrant breach of mandates issued by both the Supreme Court and the Islamabad High Court, as reported by another Pakistan-based daily, Dawn.
Article Summary: Imran Khan's sister Uzma Khan has filed a contempt of court petition in the Supreme Court. She alleges non-enforcement of previous judicial directives issued by the country's apex court. Uzma named several high-ranking officials, including Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif and Adiala (Rawalpindi Central Jail) Superintendent Sajid Baig as respondents.

Article Title: Pak pleads for dialogue after India stands firm on suspending Indus Water Treaty
Article Text:
Indus Waters treaty representational image

India rejects tribunal ruling

Water, terrorism and the SCO

NEW DELHI: Just days after India rejected an international tribunal's ruling on the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) and dismissed its jurisdiction, Pakistan on Wednesday urged New Delhi to engage "constructively" within the framework of the 1960 water-sharing agreement.According to news agency PTI, Pakistan foreign office spokesperson Tahir Andrabi said the Permanent Court of Arbitration had reaffirmed that the treaty remained fully enforced and binding. Pakistan, he said, would take “all possible measures” to ensure the decision was implemented.Andrabi said Pakistan remained committed to implementing the treaty in letter and spirit in accordance with its language and provisions.Pakistan will continue to urge India to reciprocate with the same approach whereby the treaty is upheld in letter and spirit and in its full legal documented provisions, he said, according to PTI.Pakistan had approached the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague in March 2026, seeking a determination on the status of the treaty after India placed it in abeyance.India, however, has consistently rejected the jurisdiction of the arbitration process.On Monday, the ministry of external affairs (MEA) said, “India categorically rejects its so-called award, just as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements by this illegally constituted body.”“India's decision to hold the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance remains in force,” the ministry said.MEA said the Court of Arbitration had issued what it termed an award on May 15, 2026, concerning maximum pondage supplemental to an earlier award on issues of general interpretation of the IWT."This so-called Court was constituted by the World Bank in patent breach of the terms of the Treaty and India categorically rejects its so-called award, just as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements by this illegally constituted body", the ministry stated.India has maintained that the establishment of the arbitral body itself violates the IWT and that it has no jurisdiction over India’s sovereign decision to place the treaty in abeyance.The dispute also featured indirectly at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit, in Bishkek, where Prime Minister Narendra Modi called for action against countries that use terrorism as an instrument of state policy.“We cannot remain confined to an action-reaction approach,” Modi said, calling for the dismantling of terrorist ecosystems, including funding networks, recruitment pipelines and territorial sanctuaries.Pakistan prime minister Shehbaz Sharif, speaking at the summit, described water as the region’s “lifeblood” and said it “must never be weaponised”.“The treaties governing our shared waters are solemn, binding international commitments. They are not matters of political convenience to be cast aside at your will. They must be honoured unconditionally, in both letter and spirit,” Sharif said, according to Dawn.India placed the IWT in abeyance following the April 22, 2025 Pahalgam terror attack, in which 26 people were killed. The Cabinet Committee on Security took the decision on April 23, 2025, with New Delhi saying the conditions underlying the treaty had fundamentally changed.India has said the treaty will remain in abeyance until Pakistan “credibly and irrevocably abjures its support for cross-border terrorism”.
Article Summary: Pakistan urges New Delhi to engage "constructively" within the framework of the 1960 water-sharing agreement. Pakistan had approached the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague in March 2026, seeking a determination on the status of the treaty. India, however, has consistently rejected the jurisdiction of the arbitration process.

Article Title: Leadership gaps cloud Pakistan's human rights oversight system
Article Text:
Pakistan human rights faces pending vacancy

NCHR’s legal status under question

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is most important for an effective human rights body? Strong leadership Independence Transparency Accountability 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan’s human rights oversight framework is facing growing uncertainty as key commissions continue to function without permanent leadership or full membership, raising concerns over their independence and effectiveness.The previous National Commission for Human Rights (NCHR) completed its four-year term in November 2025, but a new commission has yet to be fully constituted, news agency ANI cited in its report. The National Commission on the Status of Women (NCSW) is also functioning under an acting chairperson.Former NCHR chairperson Khawar Mumtaz criticised and warned that prolonged reliance on temporary arrangements could weaken the autonomy and performance of independent rights bodies.Human rights activist Peter Jacob said Parliament passed legislation establishing the National Commission for Minorities Rights in December 2025, but appointments to the body remain incomplete.The National Commission on the Rights of the Child has also faced vacancies. The Ministry of Human Rights invited applications in July 2026 for members representing Punjab, Islamabad and Balochistan, The Express Tribune reported.An amendment to the National Commission for Human Rights Act in 2026 introduced Section 4A, allowing a chairperson to continue for up to 120 days after the expiry of their term or until a successor is appointed.NCHR Chairperson Rabiya Javeri Agha maintained that the commission remains operationally effective, pointing to additional staff recruited two years ago. She said the extension of the chairperson’s tenure was made under the law and reflected practices followed by human rights institutions internationally. Questions regarding the constitution of a new commission, she said, should be directed to the government, according to The Express Tribune.
Article Summary: Pakistan’s human rights oversight framework is facing growing uncertainty. Key commissions continue to function without permanent leadership or full membership. The previous National Commission for Human Rights (NCHR) completed its four-year term in November 2025. A new commission has yet to be fully constituted, news agency ANI cited in its report.

Article Title: Imran Khan, wife Bushra Bibi get slight relief as Pak HC bars solitary confinement
Article Text:
Pak HC intervenes over Imran Khan, wife Bushra Bibi's detention, bars solitary confinement

A Pakistan high court on Tuesday directed authorities at Rawalpindi Jail to ensure that former prime minister Imran Khan and his wife Bushra Bibi are not held in solitary confinement. The ruling also set out provisions for Khan's family meetings, phone calls, reading material and medical care.The Islamabad High Court (IHC), while hearing petitions challenging the couple's alleged solitary confinement, directed the jail authorities to allow Khan's family members to meet him in line with prison rules and arrange telephone conversations with his sons.Justice Khadim Hussain Soomro also ordered the jail to provide Khan with newspapers and books every day and ensure access to medical facilities as prescribed under jail rules. Rawalpindi's Aiala jail superintendent has been asked to implement the directions and submit a compliance report within 15 days, according to the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).The court had earlier reserved its verdict on August 6 on separate petitions filed by Khan's sister Aleema Khanum and Bushra Bibi's daughter Mubashra Khawar Maneka. The IHC also held the petitions challenging the alleged solitary confinement to be maintainable.The 73-year-old cricketer-turned-politician and his wife have been in custody since August 2023 and is serving prison terms in corruption and related cases. Khan's Tehreek-e-Insaf party and supporters have maintained that the cases are politically motivated, while the government has rejected allegations of mistreatment.Bushra Bibi was first jailed in January 2024 after being convicted in a corruption-related case. She was released on bail in October that year after nearly nine months in custody but was arrested again in January 2025 following another corruption conviction. She remains at Adiala Jail.The IHC order comes as Khan's detention and medical treatment remain the subject of separate proceedings before the Supreme Court.On Monday, the Supreme Court declined an application by Khan's sister Uzma Khan seeking an early hearing of her contempt petition against government officials over the alleged failure to comply with an earlier order concerning his transfer to a private hospital, Dawn reported.Pakistan's Supreme Court had on August 18 ordered that Khan be shifted to the privately run Shifa International Hospital after concerns were raised by his family and supporters over his health, including an eye condition diagnosed earlier this year.Instead, Khan was taken to the state-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) on the night of August 20-21 for a medical procedure and diagnostic examinations and was later returned to Adiala Jail.Uzma Khan's petition contends that this breached the Supreme Court's direction that Khan remain admitted at the Islamabad hospital until the next hearing on September 16. The government has defended the decision, citing security concerns.Two specialists from Shifa International Hospital also participated in Khan's eye examination at PIMS, according to the hospital administration, as reported by Dawn.Uzma Khan had sought an earlier hearing, arguing that further delay could affect the enforcement of the Supreme Court's order. The Supreme Court, however, rejected the request under its case-fixation policy, noting that 94 other criminal original petitions in the same category were pending, Dawn reported.The contempt petition is listed for September 16 before a three-member bench comprising Justices Shahid Waheed, Naeem Akhtar Afghan and Ishtiaq Ibrahim. The bench is also scheduled to hear other matters concerning Khan's health and family meetings.
Article Summary: Imran Khan and his wife Bushra Bibi have been in custody since August 2023. The couple is serving prison terms in corruption and related cases. The Islamabad High Court ordered the jail authorities to allow Khan's family members to meet him in line with prison rules.

Article Title: Pakistan power crisis deepens as Karachi reels from 24-hour blackouts
Article Text:
​Karachi reels under deepening power crisis as blackouts last up to 24 hours

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you agree that electricity should be treated as an essential service? Yes No Unsure 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Karachi's electricity crisis has intensified, with residents in several parts of the city reporting outages lasting up to 24 hours. Rights activists in Pakistan have warned that prolonged loadshedding is placing a growing burden on low-income families.According to Dawn, the issue was raised at a press conference at the Karachi Press Club organised by the Civil Society Collective for Clean Energy for Karachi. Speakers said extended power cuts were disrupting basic household activities, education and work, while also worsening access to water and affecting hygiene.Residents of North Karachi, Nazimabad and parts of Gulistan-i-Jauhar reported between 16 and 24 hours of loadshedding, ANI said. Protests and traffic disruptions were also reported in Lyari and other parts of the old city during the week beginning August 24.The speakers cited K-Electric's published outage schedule, saying more than 615 feeders were listed for power cuts of up to 12 hours a day. They claimed this could affect nearly a third of the city's feeders.Qazi Khizer of the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan said the prolonged outages were having a particularly severe impact on working-class communities.He said electricity shortages were also contributing to rising mental stress and argued that reliable electricity "should be treated as an essential service rather than a privilege".Karachi Union of Journalists president Tahir Hassan Khan questioned whether K-Electric's privatisation had delivered the improvements promised to consumers.He said claims of technological and operational progress had not translated into "dependable electricity supplies".
Article Summary: Residents of North Karachi, Nazimabad and parts of Gulistan-i-Jauhar reported between 16 and 24 hours of loadshedding. Protests and traffic disruptions were also reported in Lyari and other parts of the old city during the week beginning August 24.

Article Title: Pakistan court allows Hindu woman to return home after alleged forced conversion, marriage
Article Text:
Woman returns from Pakistan

'Want to return home'

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe that the court made the right decision in allowing Reeta to return to her parents? Yes, it was the right decision. No, she should have been placed in shelter. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A court in Pakistan on Tuesday allowed a 21-year-old Hindu woman to return to her parents after she told the magistrate that she wished to go home of her own free will, days after her family alleged that she had been abducted and pressured to convert to Islam and marry a Muslim man, news agency PTI reported.Shirimati Reeta, a resident of Rana Rajput Colony in Khipro tehsil of Sindh’s Sanghar district, went missing from her hometown last week, according to a complaint filed by her brother Ravi Shankar. He alleged that CCTV footage showed unidentified people taking Reeta from the family home along with valuables and mobile phones on August 24.According to the complaint, Reeta was taken to Gujranwala in Punjab, some 80 kms from Lahore, where she was allegedly pressured to convert to Islam and marry Nazeer Hussain, who was already married.Punjab Police later recovered Reeta and produced her before a judicial magistrate on Monday. The investigating officer sought to place her in Darul Aman, a state-run shelter, claiming that she was unwilling to return to her parents.Her lawyers, Asad Jamal and Kheta Ram, opposed the request and told the court that Reeta wanted to return home with her brother, who was present in court, a court official said.The magistrate then asked Reeta to record her statement under oath. “In her statement, Reeta said that she wanted to return to her parents’ home of her own free will,” the official said.The court subsequently allowed Reeta to leave with her brother and made him responsible for her safe custody and transportation back to the family home in Sanghar.
Article Summary: Shirimati Reeta, a 21-year-old Hindu woman, went missing from her hometown last week. Her family alleged that she had been abducted and pressured to convert to Islam and marry a Muslim man. Police later recovered Reeta and produced her before a judicial magistrate on Monday. The investigating officer sought to place her in Darul Aman, a state-run shelter.

Article Title: Watch: 'Driverless' car crashes into police van after internet outage in Islamabad
Article Text:
In a social media post on Monday, Aalijah sought to clarify that his video was not intended to ridicule Zafar or undermine his work and warned that the technology was not yet ready to be considered completely reliable.

A remotely operated driverless car crashed into a police van in Islamabad after losing its internet connection during a demonstration, with footage of the incident going viral and sparking a wave of memes online.According to local media, the incident took place at D-Chowk, a high-security area in the Pakistani capital, where journalist Muhammad Aalijah was recording a video of a technology-based automated-driving system developed by Abbottabad-based technology enthusiast Ehsan Zafar. The car was being controlled remotely over the internet when a sudden connectivity failure caused its steering to malfunction.Footage shared by Aalijah shows him sitting in the front passenger seat as he explains the vehicle's features while it moves along the road. The remotely controlled steering wheel then appears to lose control, sending the car towards a police van parked nearby.Aalijah can be seen attempting to stop the vehicle by pulling the handbrake, but the car continues moving and bumps into the police vehicle.Aalijah later told Dawn that he had been asked by Zafar to report on his technology-based automated-driving innovation. He attributed the crash to a "technical fault" triggered by an internet disruption.“Everything was fine until a technical fault occurred due to an internet disruption, causing the car to go out of control and crash into a police vehicle,” he said.According to Aalijah, the vehicle was operated remotely through internet and satellite connections. The loss of the internet connection during the demonstration caused the car to become uncontrollable.In a social media post on Monday, Aalijah sought to clarify that his video was not intended to ridicule Zafar or undermine his work.“The sole purpose was to raise awareness and urge people to remain cautious until any new experiment or technology has been thoroughly tested, proven safe and established as a complete success,” he said.“This was a message of caution, not an attempt to discredit anyone.”Aalijah also warned that the technology was not yet ready to be considered completely reliable.“The vehicle was being operated through satellite and internet connections, but during external control, it went out of control as soon as the internet connection was disconnected and collided with a police vehicle,” he wrote.He said the relatively low traffic at D-Chowk limited the potential consequences of the malfunction, but warned that a similar failure on a busy road could have been far more serious.“If the same situation had occurred on a busy road, the consequences could have been extremely dangerous, even fatal,” he said.“This video is not criticism; it is a responsible effort to raise awareness and issue a warning by all means, experiment, but ensure safety first,” he added.
Article Summary: A remotely operated driverless car crashed into a police van in Islamabad after losing its internet connection during a demonstration. The incident took place at D-Chowk, a high-security area in the Pakistani capital. The car was being controlled remotely over the internet when a sudden connectivity failure caused its steering to malfunction. Footage of the incident went viral and sparked a wave of memes online.

Article Title: Pak PM scrambles for damage control after his office edits leaders out of SCO summit photo
Article Text:
The edited framing keeps Sharif at the centre alongside several prominent leaders

What’s was on the agenda

What

PM Modi

told SCO summit

Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif appeared to go into damage-control mode on Tuesday after his office shared an edited version of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit’s family photograph, cropping out several world leaders while keeping Sharif prominently at the centre of the frame.The Pakistan Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) first shared the edited summit photograph at 11:42am IST.The full image showed the heads of SCO member states and senior officials standing together ahead of a session of the 26th SCO Summit in Bishkek.From left, the photograph featured SCO Secretary-General Nurlan Yermekbayev, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Tajik President Emomali Rahmon, Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and SCO Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure chief Ularbek Sharsheev.The selective framing put Sharif at the centre of the image alongside several prominent leaders.At 3.32pm IST, the Pakistani Prime Minister shared the full family photograph featuring all the world leaders.The 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Leadership Summit focused on strengthening regional cooperation and addressing shared security, economic and geopolitical challenges.The summit, marking the SCO’s 25th anniversary was held in the expanded “SCO Plus” format, bringing together leaders from member, partner and observer countries to discuss wider regional and global issuesDuring the summit, PM Modi addressed the SCO summit and called for a united fight against terrorism, saying there could be no “double standards” on the issue.“We must dismantle the entire ecosystem of terrorism--its financing, recruitment, radicalisation, and safe havens,” Modi said, adding that countries which use terrorism as an instrument of policy and provide shelter or support to terrorists must be sent a strong message.PM Modi also called for greater regional cooperation on security, connectivity and economic opportunities, while stressing dialogue and diplomacy as the way forward in addressing conflicts.

Article Title: 100-year-old Hindu temple demolished in Pakistan’s Punjab
Article Text:
PMMP chairman Aslam Parvez Sahotra said he met Punjab Additional Home Secretary on August 28 and submitted a written application seeking action against those allegedly responsible for the demolition, as well as officials accused of failing to protect the property.
